Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)
Why was Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) called 'Sadiq' and 'Amin'? • Why is Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) called 'Rehmatul-lil-Aalamin'? • What was the impact of Hazrat Muhammad's (ﷺ) personality on people?
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

"All glory be to Allah (ﷻ). There is no God, but Allah (ﷻ) and Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) is the Rasool of Allah (ﷻ)," raised the cry from the heart of the Rasool (ﷺ) and mingled with the vast expanse of the desert of Arabia. Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) was born on Monday, the 12th of Rabi ul Awal in the year 571 AD.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

He (ﷺ) belonged to the family of Quraish, the nobility of Arabia. His family is traced back to Hazrat Ismail (علیہ السلام) and Hazrat Ibrahim (علیہ السلام). His parents died by the time he (ﷺ) was six years of age. His grandfather, Hazrat Abdul Mutalib, took charge of him but he also died soon. Now the responsibility of looking after Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) fell to his uncle Hazrat Abu Talib.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

He loved his young nephew dearly and did all he could, to rear him well. As a grown-up man, he (ﷺ) was so honourable and trustworthy that people would call him 'Al-Sadiq' and 'Al-Amin'. When Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) reached the age of 40, he (ﷺ) would
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

retire to Mount Hira for prayers and meditation. One day, while he (ﷺ) sat in a cave at Mount Hira, Hazrat Jibrail (علیہ السلام), the Angel of Revelation, appeared to him and said, "Iqra" meaning, Read! Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) said, "I am not able to read!"
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

But the command was issued twice again, each with the same response from the Rasool (ﷺ). Finally, he (ﷺ) was grasped with overwhelming force by the angel. Then Hazrat Jibrail (علیہ السلام) released him and the first verse of the Holy Quran was revealed to him.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)
"Read in the name of your lord who created."
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

Allah (ﷻ) revealed to him the true religion, Islam the belief in the total submission to 'One', 'True' and the 'Only' Allah (ﷻ), the most 'Merciful and the Mighty'. Thereafter, the Rasool (ﷺ) spared no effort in preaching the true religion Islam.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)
He (ﷺ) suffered great hardships, but nothing could move him from his path.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ) delivered his last sermon (Khutbah) on the ninth of ZulHijjah (12th and last month of the Islamic year), 10 years after Hijra (migration from Makkah Mukarammah to Madinah Munawarrah) in the Uranah Valley of Mount Arafat. His words were quite clear and concise and were directed to the entire humanity.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

"O People, lend me an attentive ear, for I know not whether after this year, I shall ever be amongst you again. Therefore, listen to what I am saying to you very carefully and take these words to those who could not be present here today.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)
Beware of Satan! for the safety of your religion. Your lives and property are a sacred trust amongst yourselves until you appear before your Lord, and
Note

Think
What did the Prophet mean when he says that every right arising out of homicide in pre-Islamic days is waived?
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

remember you shall have to appear before your Lord, who shall demand from you an account of all your actions. You have rights over your wives and your wives have rights over you. Treat them with kindness and affection. Be faithful to each other and do not commit sins. Allah (ﷻ) has forbidden you to take usury (interest); therefore, all interest obligations shall henceforth be waived.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

No murders committed during the days of ignorance (Jahiliyyat) are to be avenged. Do not forget that every Muslim should be truly a brother to every other Muslim. There is no preference for the Arab over the non- Arab or the non-Arab over the Arab, also a white has no superiority over black nor does a black have any superiority over white. Only the goodness and piety of a man makes him superior to others.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

O People! listen to me in earnest, worship Allah (ﷻ), say your five prayers (Salah) daily, fast during the month of Ramadan, and give your wealth in Zakat. Perform Hajj if you can afford it. Feed and clothe your slaves with such food as you eat yourself and with such clothes as you wear yourself. If they commit a fault, which you find hard to forgive, then let them go away and do not treat them harshly.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)
Be kind and just to everyone.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)

O People! No Nabi or Rasool will come after me and no new faith will be born. Reason well, therefore, O people! and understand words which I convey to you. I leave behind me two things, the 'Qur'an' and my 'Sunnah' and if you follow these, you will never go astray. Have I fulfilled my mission?," said he (ﷺ) addressing the assembled people.
Reading: The Last Sermon of Hazrat Muhammad (ﷺ)
"In truth you have," replied the hundreds of the pilgrims. "Be my witness, O Allah (ﷻ)! that I have conveyed your message to your people".

Listening
In pairs, talk about the following questions.
Listening

What comes to your mind when you hear the word 'Nature'? • What is the most beautiful thing in nature for you? Why? • Where is nature at its most beautiful-the mountains, oceans, desert, beaches, space or forests? Why do you think so? • How could the world be a better place if we all went back to nature?
Note
Take turns and read this text aloud. Be sensitive to other speakers. Do not speak when someone else is speaking. You need to listen carefully when someone is speaking aloud.
Listening
Listen to the audio clips from the perspective of Nature.
Announcement

Some call me Nature. Others call me Mother Nature. I've been here for over four and a half billion years, 22500 times longer than you. I don't really need people, but people need me. Yes, your future depends on me. When I thrive you thrive, when I falter you falter, or worse. But I've been here for aeons. I have fed species greater than you, and I have starved species greater than you.
Announcement

My oceans, my soil, my flowing streams, my forests: they all can take you or leave you. Whether you regard or disregard me doesn't really matter to me. One way or the other, your actions will determine your fate, not mine. I am nature. I will go on. I am prepared to evolve. Are you, too?
Announcement

Look up! There I am. I am the sky. I am a warm, protective blanket wrapped over everyone on Earth. I can bring clouds, rain and the wind. I can be an ice storm. Without me, you'd fry. Every day I am the breath you take in. Yet, you are making me sick. I am congested, off-balance, and polluted. You see. I am more delicate than you think.
Announcement

It took millions of years to get it just right, my perfect mix of gases, temperature and weather that you enjoy. But now your cars, your factories and dust have pushed me past the limit. And you wonder why my typhoons and tornadoes are more intense, more frequent. I have become unpredictable. less rain here, a lot more rain there, hotter summers, colder winters. I cannot even control myself anymore. Enough about me.
Announcement
I will show my changing self to you in the days ahead. But in the end, I'll be fine. Give me a few thousand years. I have weathered trauma before. I am not worried for myself. Look up!

Use of Language
An adjective is a word that describes a noun or a pronoun. They allow for the description of what they are modifying, therefore forming a more vivid image of what is being described.
Use of Language
Quantitative Adjective shows how much of anything is described. It is further divided into;
Use of Language
Definitive: It shows an exact number like one, two, second etc. Example: I have been here for over four and a half billion years.
Use of Language
Indefinite: It shows the quantity which is not an exact count like all, few, several, some, many, certain etc. Example: Some of you keep me protected.
Use of Language
Distributive: It shows a specific number out of a group, such as each, every, neither, etc. Example: Each one of us should protect nature.

Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

Text 2A — Read about an educational trip to the Khewra mines. Each paragraph provides certain information. Read the passage to identify the main idea of each paragraph and try to describe it in your own words.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

Nature and natural resources always fascinate me. Last week, my family and I planned a trip to the Khewra mines. It was a pleasant morning in March. I was so excited that I could hardly sleep at night. At 6:30 am, we started our journey from Islamabad.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder
It was almost 11: 30 am when we reached there. The weather was clear and the sun was shining brightly. I was greatly fascinated to stand in front of the world's second-largest salt mines.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder
The Khewra Salt Mines are situated on the right bank of the Jhelum River. The main tunnel was developed by a British mining engineer, Dr. H. Warth.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

On entering the mines, I saw a spectacular view in front of me. It seemed as if I have entered into a beautiful panorama. I always wanted to ride a mining train, and my wish came true here. The electric train that runs from the entrance of the mine to the main hall is said to be from the 1930s when mining first began at Khewra. It is in perfect working condition and a per-person ticket is charged to travel.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder
The train ride took us to the assembly hall where more wonders were waiting for us.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

Khewra Mines is also home to miniature replicas of famous monuments built and craved entirely from rock salt. Among these are 'The Great Wall of China', 'Minar-e-Pakistan', the 'Shimla Hill of Lahore', the 'Mall of Murree' and 'Badshahi Masjid'. The beautiful replica of Badshahi Masjid is built well within central chamber and is entirely made of rock salt bricks of varying colours.
Points to know!

There are various levels of salt mine where extraction takes place, out of which six are below the surface. Over 850,000 tons of rock salt is produced annually by these stunning natural sights. The mine, which receives up to 250,000 tourists a year, is well known for producing pink Khewra salt, which is frequently sold under the name Himalayan salt.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder
Each of these monuments has also been lit up brilliantly to increase the beauty of multi-coloured salt.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

My amazement did not end here. There was more to come. I had never heard about a salt fountain. Although there was no salt flowing out of the fountain, the natural shape this salt formation has taken over the years makes it look like a flowing water fountain. The salt bridge was one of my favourites. Also known as Pul- Saraat, this is a 25-feet long narrow bridge built over a 100-feet deep pond of salt water.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

What's unique about this bridge is that it is made purely of salt and uses no columns or pillars for support. Lastly, we saw the beautiful Sheesh Mahal. A tunnel within the mines known as the 'Palace of Mirrors' or 'Sheesh Mahal', not because it contains the monument of a palace but because the salt roof of the tunnel shines like mirrors. The tunnel can be explored as part of the guided tour.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder

I was truly amazed at the beauty of nature. Never did I imagine salt to be so beautiful and colourful. It turned out to be a memorable day as we had fun and awareness at the same time. The structure of the Khewra mines is quite stable and offers a opportunity to explore a different world underground. So pack for a day trip to explore the wonders of this tourist destination to your heart's content.
Reading: A Visit to Khewra Mines - A Natural Wonder
Do not forget to bring back a salt lamp as a souvenir. They not only have healing properties but are used as gifts for loved ones.
Points to know!
Punctuation cues such as commas help in reading. They help the reader to clearly understand the message being conveyed. Read the passage and identify how these cues help you read better.
While Reading
The author has used a number of words to describe his feelings and excitement. Can you identify them while reading? Underline them and try to use them while describing your own feelings.
Forms and Degrees of Adjectives:

Regular Adjectives: Regular adjectives follow a consistent pattern when forming their comparative and superlative degrees. They usually add "-er" to form the comparative degree and "-est" to form the superlative degree. For example, "tall" (comparative: taller, superlative: tallest) or "big" (comparative: bigger, superlative: biggest).
Forms and Degrees of Adjectives:

Irregular Adjectives: Irregular adjectives do not follow the standard pattern for forming comparative and superlative degrees. They have unique forms for each degree and don't rely on adding "-er" or "-est." For example, "good" (comparative: better, superlative: best) or "bad" (comparative: worse, superlative: worst).
Forms and Degrees of Adjectives:

Absolute Adjectives: Absolute adjectives do not vary in degree. They describe qualities that are considered absolute and cannot be compared. These adjectives do not have comparative or superlative forms. For example, "perfect," "unique," or "dead."
Forms and Degrees of Adjectives:
Positive Degree: The positive degree of an adjective is the base form or the simplest form of the adjective. It does not indicate any comparison. For example, "tall," "beautiful," or "fast."
Forms and Degrees of Adjectives:

Comparative Degree: The comparative degree of an adjective is used to compare two things or people. It shows a higher or lower degree of a particular quality compared to another. For example, "taller," "more beautiful," or "faster."
Forms and Degrees of Adjectives:

Superlative Degree: The superlative degree of an adjective is used to compare more than two things or people. It indicates the highest or lowest degree of a particular quality within a group. For example, "tallest," "most beautiful," or "fastest."
Personal Recount

A recount tells an experience or an event that happened in the past. The purpose of a recount can be to inform, entertain or to reflect and evaluate. A recount can focus on a specific section of an event or retell the entire story. A recount should be told in the order that things happened. A personal recount retells an activity the writer has been personally involved in.
Tips to write a well-constructed personal recount
Orientation: WHO was involved? WHAT happened? WHERE did this event take place? WHEN and HOW did it happen?
Tips to write a well-constructed personal recount
Sequence Of Events: Important events in ORDER they happened.
Tips to write a well-constructed personal recount
Use PAST TENSE e.g. had, ate. Use FIRST PERSON e.g. I or We, if you are involved or THIRD PERSON if you are not involved.

Eid:
Muslims across the world celebrate two Eids respectively known as Eid-ul-Fitr and Eid-ul-Adha.
Eid:

Eid-ul-Fitr is a festival that marks the end of Ramadan, the ninth month of the Islamic calendar. During the holy month of Ramadan, Muslims do not eat or drink anything during daylight hours. Eid-ul-Fitr, therefore, celebrates the end of a month of fasting. Its name means "Festival of Breaking Fast" in Arabic.
Eid:

Muslims begin the festival by praying together at dawn on the first day. Later, families gather to enjoy special meals and sweets. Children wear new clothes, and gifts are exchanged. People also visit the graves of their relatives. Some cities hold elaborate outdoor ceremonies.
Eid:

Eid-ul-Adha is an important festival in Islam. It is held each year to commemorate Hazrat Ibrahim's (علیہ السلام) devotion to Allah (ﷻ) and his readiness to sacrifice his son, Hazrat Ismail (علیہ السلام). The name Eid-ul-Adha means "Festival of Sacrifice" in Arabic.
Eid:

It is a time for prayer, visiting with friends and family, and giving gifts. Many families also sacrifice an animal in commemoration of Hazrat Ibrahim's (علیہ السلام) sacrifice. Then they distribute the meat among family members, friends, neighbours, and the poor.
Chinese New Year:

Chinese New Year is the mot important celebration in the Chinese Calendar. It is also known as the spring festival because it celebrates the start of new life and the season for planting crops. The Chinese new year begins in late January or early February. The fifteen-day celebration begins with the new moon and lasts until the full moon.
Chinese New Year:

The last event of the fifteen-day celebration is the Lantern Festival. People often hang glowing lanterns in temples or carry them during a night time parade. The dragon dance highlights celebrations in many areas. A long, colourful dragon is carried through streets by numerous dancers.

Conjunctions:
Conjunctions are words which connects words, phrases and clauses in a sentence. A few examples are given below.
Conjunctions:

and: to connect similar or related ideas. Example: I like to read books and watch movies. • too: to add another similar idea or action. Example: She enjoys playing basketball. I do too. • as well as: to add additional information. Example: He speaks Spanish as well as French. • although: introduce a contrasting idea or condition. Example: Although it was raining, we still went for a walk. • but:
Conjunctions:

introduce a contrasting idea or condition. Example: She studied hard, but she still failed the test. • however: to indicate a contrasting idea or condition. Example: It was a difficult task; however, she managed to complete it. • because: to indicate a reason or cause. Example: I stayed at home because I wasn't feeling well. • in order to: to express purpose or intention. Example:
Conjunctions:

He saved money in order to buy a new car. • where: indicate a place or location. Example: We visited a park where we could have a picnic. • wherever: to indicate any place or location. Example: She can work from home wherever she is. • if: to introduce a conditional clause. Example: If it rains, we will stay indoors. • until: to indicate the duration of an action or condition. Example: You won't pass the test unless you study. • therefore: used to indicate a cause-and-effect relationship or conclusion. Remember!

The Spring Festival-To celebrate the advent of spring, two very important events are organised to activate the cultural aspects, Jashn-e-Baharan and Horse and Cattle Show. These shows not only serve the purpose of celebrating spring but also reflects the unification of different cultures in Pakistan.
The Spring Festival
The festival lasts for a month and includes Sufi nights, light shows, poetry evening, flower display and several other events.
The Shandur Polo Festival

The Shandur Polo Festival is an amazing festival celebrated by the tribes of Gilgit and Chitral in the northern areas of Pakistan. The tribes from the regions of Gilgit-Baltistan and Chitral meets at the Shandur pass every summer. The festival invites visitors to experience a traditional Polo tournament. The festival also includes folk music, dancing, and a camping village set up.
Sindhi Cultural Day

Sindhi Cultural Day-A popular Sindhi cultural festival, also known as 'Aekta Jo Dihaarro' it is widely celebrated with traditional enthusiasm to spotlight the centuries-old rich culture of Sindh. The day is celebrated all over Sindh on the first Sunday of December. On the occasion, people wear the Ajrak, Sindhi Topi and the traditional block printed shawl.
Sindhi Cultural Day
Musical programmes and rallies are held in many cities to mark the day with zeal.
The Kashmir Cultural Festival

The Kashmir Cultural Festival-The culture of Kashmir is a blend of multiple customs. To promote solidarity with Kashmiri people, Lok Virsa organises a festival each year on the 5th of February each year. The day-long festival aims to provide a platform to the Kashmiri artists and craftsmen to present the Kashmiri culture to the world.
The Kalat Festival

The Kalat Festival is named after a district in Balochistan, previously known as Qalat. The festival is celebrated every year in October. It has a unique significance since it presents a much needed opportunity to gather people from around the world and Pakistan to connect in a peaceful event and explore the hidden treasures of Balochistan and its centuries-old culture.
The Kalat Festival

The Balochi festival also has the potential to empower the feelings of brotherhood, compassion, and love through vibrant colours, soulful music, and other such festivities. Along with leaving a lasting impression, the Kalat Festival also contributes highly towards highlighting the fact that every human, regardless of all other factors, want the same things in life:
The Kalat Festival
peace, security, a tune to sing and dance to, and a delicious serving of food.
Kalam Festival

Kalam Festival, Kalam Mela or Swat Summer Festival is a cultural event and a vibrant celebration that takes place in the month of July or August in Kalam and Mahodand. It is the biggest cultural festival of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa. The festival starts with a grand opening ceremony, characterized by colourful processions, traditional music, and dance performances that set the stage for the days to come.
Kalam Festival
Food, music, bustling marketplace, with a range of handicrafts, intricate embroidery, and traditional garments. The festival has become a symbol of unity, togetherness and peace for the region.
The Kalash Festivals

The Kalash Festivals - Kalash festivities are well-known across the world. Three festivals that are more significant are observed in various months of the year. The most significant event, Chilam Joshi, lasts for four days, in May. The Chitirmas Festival, is held in the winter. The Kalasha tribe celebrates the Choimus Festival, which is a colourful whirl of traditional dances, foods, and chants of worship.
The Kalash Festivals

In August, people celebrate the Kalash Uchal Festival when they harvest their crops. Singing, dancing, and thanking nature for providing them with the barley and wheat harvest season are the main highlights of the festival. For the Uchal festival, special dishes such as cheese, buttermilk, and cornbread are made.

Reading: The Endangered Animals of Pakistan

Pakistan is home to versatile and potent wildlife, which sadly, is running low in numbers. Endangered species all over the world get special attention and security – whilst the Pakistani animals strive to survive in these challenging conditions. Let's take a look at some of these amazing animals that are in the danger of extinction.
Did you Know?

People all over the world are working to help save endangered animals from extinction. There are conservation organisations which try to make people aware of the problems facing wild animals. Some of the ways in which they are being saved include habitat protection, captive breeding, setting up nature reserves and parks and using alternative products in place of products from rare animals.
Indus River Dolphin

Indus river dolphins are believed to have originated in the ancient Tethys Sea. When the sea dried up approximately 50 million years ago, the dolphins were forced to adapt to its only remaining habitat—rivers. The Indus River Dolphin is found in the Lower Indus Basin. These friendly creatures are often seen jumping around boats and putting on performances for anyone that wants to watch.
Woolly Flying Squirrel

The Gilgit region is home to the nocturnal rodent, Woolly Flying Squirrel. This unique creature looks like a bat but is actually a squirrel. The flying squirrel is one of the largest squirrels in the world with 1.5 to 2 feet in height. Due to loss of natural habitat they are now labeled as critically endangered species.
The Markhor

The Markhor is the national animal of Pakistan. It is the largest of the goat family and is commonly found in the Northern Areas of Pakistan and Balochistan. The name Markhor translates to "snake eater" in Persian, for the Markhor holds great skill at killing snakes in the wild to protect its partner. Despite their large size, Markhors are extremely skilled climbers.
The Markhor
They can climb trees and other slanted structures, including dangerous cliffs, in search of food and to avoid predators.
Snow Leapard

Native to the mountainous regions of Khyber Pakhtunkhwa, this ferocious animal is the National Heritage Animal of Pakistan. Although smaller than the other "big cats", the Snow Leopard weighs about 30-70 kg.
Soft Shelled Turtle

The Soft Shelled Turtle or Trionychidae is one of the rarest types of turtle to have been found on Pakistan soil. This amazing reptile with its elongated snorkel like nostrils and leathery shell is quite unique and easily distinguishable from other turtles.
Balochistan Forest Dormouse
It is a species of rodent in the family Gliridae. It is native to Pakistan found near Ziarat, Balochistan. It is an endangered animal.
Black Finless Porpoise

It is found in the coastal belts of Indo-Pak borders. The finless porpoise is often caught in fishing nets across the coasts of Pakistan. Other threats to the species include habitat loss, boat traffic, and pollution.
Moon Bear

The Moon bear makes its home in the Himalayas. Known as the Asian Black Bear, the crescent shaped, white patch on the chest has led to it being called the Moon Bear. Although herbivore by nature, it can be quite aggressive when defending its territory.

What do you know about extreme weather on Earth? • What is climate? How does climate relate to weather? • What is global warming? • What are the causes of global warming?
Reading: Extreme Weather

As the Earth has warmed, climate change has triggered many threats to our planet. Extreme weather and catastrophic events, such as heat waves, droughts, floods, heavy downpours, tornadoes, hurricanes, storms, blizzards and more are the result of climate change. Here are some of the extreme weather and climate conditions the world is experiencing.
Did you Know?
Weather describes conditions in the atmosphere over a short period of time. Climate describes weather patterns of a particular region over a longer period, usually 30 years or more.
Tornadoes

Tornadoes are a type of extreme weather. They are vertical funnels of rapidly spinning air. Tornadoes include clouds, strong wind, rain, and sometimes hail. They move at a speed of about 16 to 32 kilometres per hour (10 to 20 miles per hour), and their winds can top 402 kilometres per hour (250 miles per hour).
Hurricanes

Due to global warming, global climate models predict hurricanes which likely cause more intense rainfall and have an increased coastal flood risk due to a higher storm surge caused by rising seas. Additionally, the global frequency of storms may decrease or remain unchanged, but hurricanes that form are more likely to become intense.
Flood

Floods are caused or amplified by both natural and man made factors. Major weather factors include heavy or prolonged precipitation, snow melt, thunderstorms, storm surges from hurricanes, and ice or debris jams. Human factors include structural failures of dams and levees, altered drainage, and land cover alterations (such as pavement).
Heat Waves

Heat waves are periods of abnormally hot weather lasting days to weeks. The number of heat waves has been increasing in recent years. This trend has continued over the years, with the number of intense heat waves being trippled. The recent heat waves and droughts in many countries have set records for the highest monthly average temperatures.
Heat Waves
Analyses show that human-induced climate change has generally increased the probability of heat waves.
Drought

Higher temperatures lead to increased rates of evaporation, including more loss of moisture through plant leaves. As soil dries out, a larger proportion of the incoming heat from the sun absorbs heating the soil and adjacent air rather than evaporating its moisture, resulting in hotter summers under drier climatic conditions.
Use of Language
A transitive verb is a verb that requires an object to receive the action. He played the piano. The wind can top 402 kilometres per hour.
Use of Language
An intransitive verb does not take an object. The soil dries out. She slept all day.

Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

The importance of the natural environment in providing the foundation for human well-being, development and resilience cannot be denied. But it is equally important to protect the environment. Heavily populated cities have the potential to destroy all kinds of plants and animal habitats but they are particularly threatening the fragile ecosystem such as rainforests.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

Measures are being taken to protect the environment. A number of countries are working to make their cities resilient and sustainable. These cities are also called future cities. Carbon free transport, garbage-free streets, plentiful water supplies, etc. are some of the goals of future cities.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities
Countries are coming up with innovative ideas to convert waste and garbage into fertilisers and using them in constructing modern carbon-free buildings. One example is the ancient city of Venlo.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

The ancient city of Venlo in the Netherlands has embraced the principles of "cradle-to-cradle" (C2C) in all of its new construction. Every material must be reusable, with none going to the landfill and no loss of quality. So when the centuries-old town hall needed renovating, city leaders chose instead to build a brand new one, which opened in 2016.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities
It showcases the benefits of a C2C design, puts the city on the path to a circular economy, and acts as a model for cities around the world that want to go waste free.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities
The town hall boasts truly healthy air; thanks to several innovations. Its solar chimney warms incoming air, creating a natural draft; no mechanical ventilation is necessary.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities
The top floor is a greenhouse that adds oxygen and humidity to the air before it flows throughout the building. The building itself includes atriums, which aid air flow and provide natural light.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

The entire northern facade of the town hall is a vertical garden. The plants provide city birds and insects a place to rest and breed. More than 100 different plants convert carbon dioxide into oxygen and clean particulates out of the air. The plants also absorb the nitrogen generated by nearby cars and trains, making the city air cleaner. The plants also insulate the building from heat, cold, and noise.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

There are even green walls in the parking garage as well as raised areas with ferns and gradually decomposing logs. The plants do their work of cleaning and humidifying the air of the parking garage, and you can even pick edible mushrooms off the walls!
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

Engineers in Europe are experimenting with building materials that are sustainable and more energy efficient. They are using the bio composite of dried orange peels and clay. Wall making with it and a second layer of rammed earth, a traditional building material, have greater insulating properties than lightweight concrete. The houses are much more comfortable and save energy.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities

A construction company in England combines orange peels with other kinds of food waste to make a strong building material similar to fibreboard. The company is partnering with engineers, designers, and scientists to transform the construction industry by phasing out fossil-fuel materials entirely and replacing them with bioengineered materials like the orange peels.
Reading: Preparing for Future Waste Free Cities
Making our cities waste-free is extremely important as it will improve the environment and reduce pollution.

Use of Language

A pronoun is a word that stands in place of a noun. There are different types of pronouns. Personal pronouns are used in place of the person, place or thing that we are talking about. We can use personal pronouns as a subject and as an object of a sentence. Their form changes to indicate a person, number, gender, or case.
Use of Language

Type | Example; Subjective personal pronouns (I, you, she, he, it, you, and they) | I decided to work as a ship's doctor.; Objective personal pronouns (me, you, her, him, it, us, you, and them) | The ship hit a rock in the sea, and it began to sink.; Possessive personal pronouns (mine, yours, hers, his, its, ours, and theirs) | The ship was ours.
Use of Language
Indefinite pronouns are those referring to one or more unspecified objects, beings, or places. Examples: anyone, somebody, whichever, whoever, other, something, nobody. Everyone was drowned.
Use of Language

Reflexive pronouns are the pronouns preceded by the adverb, adjective, pronoun, or noun to which they refer, and ending in –self or –selves. Examples: Myself, yourself, himself, herself, itself, ourselves, yourselves, themselves. Lemuel Gulliver couldn't blame himself.
Use of Language
Demonstrative pronouns are those used to point to something specific within a sentence. Examples: this, that, these, those. This creature was really a tiny man.
Use of Language

Reciprocal Pronouns are used when two or more people or things are doing the same action to each other. They show a mutual or reciprocal relationship. The two common reciprocal pronouns are 'each other' and 'one another.' Example: Maheen and Ayesha always help each other with their homework.
Use of Language

Interrogative pronouns are those which introduce a question. We can usually identify interrogative pronouns by the fact that they often appear at the beginning of a question. Examples: who, whom, whose, what, which. Who had tried to hurt me with their arrows?

Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

The cornerstone of modern life has transformed the way world communicates personally and in business. From switchboards and satellites to copper wire and fibre optics or the nearly instant internet connections, engineers continue to answer the call for innovation. But probably one innovation is said to change the face of the world.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

Like many inventions, the telephone was likely thought of many years before it was invented, and by many people. But it wasn't until 1876 when Alexander Graham Bell patented the telephone and was allowed to start selling it.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

One of the first types of telephones to become popular in the 1890s looked like the one in the picture. There were two main pieces: the speaker, which you would hold up to your ear to hear, and the mouthpiece, which you would hold up to your mouth to talk into. People would move the little wheel at the bottom to dial a phone number.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

The first telephones were large and awkward, and each was powered by its own battery. Battery power couldn't carry voices very far, however. That problem was solved in the 1890s, when telephone networks began using outside power sources. Electrical impulses transmitted speech over long distances through the wires of a "landline system" using phones that could not be moved from the place where they were installed.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

In the beginning, a user began a phone call by speaking to an operator. It was the operator's job to connect one phone to another. After the early 1920s, though, rotary phones became common. Rotary phones had dials that let users enter number combinations to contact other users. During the 1960s and 1970s, dials were largely replaced by the "touch-tone" keypads that remain standard today.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

Mobile phones powered completely by batteries appeared in the mid-1980s, bypassing landline systems altogether. Conversations were instead transmitted through signals coordinated by satellite-based systems. The earliest mobile phones were big and ugly and costed thousands of dollars. But by the mid-1990s, they had gotten much smaller (and cheaper) and were called cellular (or cell) phones.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

Telephones took an altogether new look in the recent past. Without a doubt, they have become more powerful and smarter than ever before. Most of us nowadays carry the world in our pocket! It is amazing but true. A mobile phone can make us connected to the rest of the world within seconds.
Reading: Telephones-Then and Now

Today, phones take pictures, connect us to the Internet, and even enable us to see one another as we converse. Advances continue at a rate that is impossible to keep track of or predict. How will we all be communicating in another 10 years, you might ask? Well... just keep watching and listening!

Text 7C — Children possesses an unmatched sense of wonder and possibility. To them, the world feels endless and beautiful. With their matchless energies, they can come up with the most amazing ideas and inventions. You may be surprised to discover that a number of inventions that we know and love today were hatched in the minds of children.
Frank Epperson: Popsicle

Eleven-year-old Frank Epperson invented what we've come to know as a popsicle. It was a winter's eve in 1905 when Frank decided to mix a frozen concoction containing soda powder and water. He accidentally left the drink outside overnight, with the stirring stick in the glass. The mixture froze and the first popsicle was created.
Frank Epperson: Popsicle

Though this was where it began, the treat didn't gain notoriety until 1922 when Epperson gave it out at a fireman's ball. He originally patented the idea under, "Eppsicle," but changed it after his children started calling it a "popsicle." So, funnily enough, kids came up with both the idea and the name.
Louis Braille: Braille

Louis Braille suffered a serious eye injury when he was just 3 years old. Not only did the accident render him blind on that eye, the infection spread and blinded the other eye as well. After more than a decade of struggling with the slow system of tracing his finger over raised letters, Braille was 12 when he learned of a method of silent communication originally created for the French military.
Louis Braille: Braille
He simplified it, and in 1824 the Braille language was born.
Water Talkie

In 1996, fifth grader Richie Stachowski invented the Water Talkie, a device that allows people to talk to each other underwater. It was a hit, so Stachowski expanded his product line under a company he called Short Stack. In 1999, he sold his product to a company in millions.
George Nissen: Trampoline

George invented the trampoline in 1930 at the age of 16. He came up with the idea after seeing trapeze artists drop into a net at the end of their performance. He thought the act would be more exciting if they kept bouncing around so he began working in his parent's garage. He improved his design over the years to what it looks like now. Today, trampoline is one of children's favourite bouncing thing.
Chester Greenwood: Earmuffs

It was 1873 and Chester Greenwood was just 15 years old when his ears got painfully cold one day while ice skating. He found that wrapping a scarf around his head didn't help much, so he decided to find a better solution. Greenwood designed a wire frame and had his grandmother sew tufts of beaver's fur between loops of wire to it, thereby making the first pair of earmuffs.
Phrasal Verbs

Phrasal verbs are two or more words that act together as a completely new word, with a meaning separate from the original words. A phrasal verb combines a normal verb with an adverb or a preposition to create an entirely new verbal phrase—the phrasal verb.

The meaning of a phrasal verb is usually unrelated to the meanings of the words that comprise it, so think of a phrasal verb as an entirely new and independent word. For example, scroll and up have two different meanings but when combined together, they mean 'move text on the screen.'

1.1 Plant Systems
Plants have only two systems i.e. Root system and shoot system.
1.2 Root System

Have you ever wondered why the whole plant does not blow away with the wind? This is due to the roots of the plant. The roots of a plant spread in the soil and anchor it. They absorb water and minerals from the soil by the process of diffusion. There are many tiny root hairs on the epidermis which help in the absorption. Vascular bundle including xylem and phloem is present in the centre of roots.
1.2 Root System
Cortex is present between epidermis and vascular bundle.
1.2 Root System

There are two main types of roots: taproots and fibrous roots. A taproot system has one main root called primary root that grows downward. Many smaller roots branch out from the primary root known as secondary roots. The branches of secondary roots are called tertiary roots. Taproots are found in many plants, trees and shrubs.
1.2 Root System
While fibrous roots are thread like structures that spread out from the base of the stem of a plant e.g. grasses and wheat.
Do You Know?
Aerial roots are roots that grow on the parts of a plant above the ground. The aerial roots in Banyan mature into thick, woody trunks and help the tree spread over a wide area.
1.3 Shoot System
Shoot system has stem, leaves, flowers and fruits.
1.3 Shoot System
Stem: The stem gives support to the plant. It transports substances between the roots and aerial parts of the plant including leaves, flowers and fruits.
1.3 Shoot System

Two main types of stem are herbaceous stem and woody stem. Plants with green and flexible stems are called herbaceous (e.g. daisies, grass and cereals) while plants with hard and strong stems are called woody plants (e.g. trees and shrubs).
1.3 Shoot System
In a stem, vascular bundles are arranged, just beneath the epidermis. The vascular bundles are strong and provide support to the plant. Pith is present in the centre for storage.
Do You Know?
In desert plants like Cactus thick stems store water and are green to perform photosynthesis.
Interesting Facts
Sargodha has the largest tree in Pakistan. This Banyan tree is amazing with over one thousand roots and covers an area of approximately three acres.
1.4 Leaves

Leaf consists of two parts i.e. leaf blade and leaf stalk. The flat green portion of a leaf is called leaf blade. Each leaf has a central midrib and many veins. Midrib is the extension of leaf stalk. The midrib and veins provide support to the leaf. They contain vascular bundles to transport substances to and from the leaves.
1.4 Leaves

The process of photosynthesis takes place in mesophyll of leaves. The outer most layer of a leaf is epidermis. There is a water proof covering over epidermis called cuticle. Gases move in and out through small holes in the leaf epidermis, called stomata. Surrounding each stoma is a pair of guard cells. The two guard cells work together to open and close the stomata.
1.4 Leaves
Stomata open during day time and close at night time.
1.5 Transport
Transportation is the movement of materials from one place to another. The transport system of a plant consists of network of tubes called xylem and phloem.
1.5 Transport

Xylem: The xylem transports water and dissolved minerals from the roots to the leaves through the stem. They have thick and strong walls which support the plant. Xylem is a dead tissue. In trees new xylem is made each year forming rings in the tree trunk. Xylem forms wood.
1.5 Transport
Phloem: The phloem transports food in the form of sugar solution from leaves to all other parts of the plant. Sugar solution can go up and down the phloem at the same time.
1.6 Transpiration

The loss of water from the stomata in the leaf is called transpiration. As the water evaporates from the leaves, more is pulled up through the xylem to replace it. The main force which draws water up the plant is called transpiration pull.
1.6 Transpiration
When water loss is more than the water intake by a plant, it will wilt. It mostly happens on a hot, dry, sunny day.
1.6 Transpiration
The light intensity, temperature, humidity, wind and water supply will all affect the transpiration rate.

1.7 Photosynthesis

Leaves and other parts of the plant are green because of chlorophyll. It is a green pigment that absorbs light energy and is present in the chloroplast of the plant cell. It enables a plant to make its own food by the process of photosynthesis. During photosynthesis, plants use light energy from the sun, carbon dioxide from the air and water from the soil to make glucose and oxygen.
1.7 Photosynthesis

Carbon dioxide enters the leaf through stomata and water comes from xylem to the leaf cells. The glucose produced is transported to all parts of the plant. Oxygen is also produced by photosynthesis. Plant cells use some of the oxygen for respiration, extra oxygen moves out through stomata.
Teaching Point
All life forms depend on the process of photosynthesis for food and oxygen. It is the only source of oxygen on planet earth.
1.8 Leaves as Best Photosynthesis Sites
Leaf structure is best suited for the process of photosynthesis due to the following adaptations:
1.8 Leaves as Best Photosynthesis Sites

Broad and flat shape to help absorption of sunlight and carbon dioxide • Thin to help diffusion of gases • Large air spaces for easy movement of gases • Large number of stomata for exchange of gases • Network of veins to supply water to the cells • Transparent epidermis to allow entry of light • Waxy cuticle to slow water loss • Large number of chloroplasts in photosynthetic cells
1.9 Minerals for Plant Growth

Do you like to grow plants? Growing healthy plants is not always easy! They require water, sunlight, air and some minerals as well. Plants need nitrates to make proteins which help to form new cells and tissues. For photosynthesis they need magnesium to make chlorophyll.

1.10 Respiration

Living things get energy from their food by the process called cellular respiration. In plant cells glucose reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide, water and energy. Carbon dioxide and water are the waste products. This process mainly takes place in the mitochondria.
1.10 Respiration

Plant cells respire all the time, so they need continuous supply of oxygen. During day time, they make more oxygen by photosynthesis so extra oxygen goes into air. At night, photosynthesis stops, so plants take in oxygen and give out carbon dioxide like animals.

Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration
Our body needs energy for doing different functions, for example playing:
Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

All our energy comes from the food we eat. The food we eat is broken down into small molecules like glucose. Cells use glucose to get energy. Energy is released from food by the process of cellular respiration. Cellular respiration is a series of chemical reactions which slowly releases energy stored in the food molecules. It is essential for the survival of every living cell.
Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration
It occurs continuously throughout the life.
2.1 Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

Cellular respiration is of two types. It can take place with or without oxygen. If it takes place in the presence of oxygen, it is called aerobic respiration. During aerobic respiration glucose reacts with oxygen in mitochondria of cells to release large amount of energy. Carbon dioxide and water are produced as the waste products.
2.1 Aerobic and Anaerobic Respiration

If oxygen is not available, then some cells temporarily shift to anaerobic respiration. This releases a small amount of energy from food as compared to aerobic respiration. Waste products can be lactic acid or alcohol and carbon dioxide.
2.2 Human Respiratory System

Respiratory system helps in the process of breathing and exchange of gases. It consists of air ways and lungs. Air enters in nasal cavity through nostrils. In the nasal cavity the air becomes clean, warm and moist. Then air passes through larynx and enters in the trachea. Trachea divides into two bronchi which enter into lungs. Inside lungs the bronchi further branch into bronchioles.
2.2 Human Respiratory System
Bronchioles end at tiny, thin walled air sacs called alveoli. Exchange of gases between air and blood takes place at alveoli. Lung is like a huge sponge as it contains millions of alveoli.
2.2 Human Respiratory System

Exchange of Gases: Oxygen from the inhaled air diffuses from alveoli to the blood in the capillaries. This oxygenated blood is carried to the cells in other parts of the body. The waste product of cellular respiration i.e. carbon dioxide is added to the blood. This deoxygenated blood (blood with less oxygen and more carbon dioxide) reaches lungs. Carbon dioxide from blood capillaries diffuses into alveoli air.
2.2 Human Respiratory System
Eventually the carbon dioxide is breathed out of the body.
Do You Know?
Alveoli are perfect respiratory surfaces as they · are thin walled (single cell thickness) · have a large surface area · are moist · are surrounded by blood capillaries · have a supply of fresh air
Interesting Facts
If all alveoli of your lungs are flattened and put together, their surface area will be equal to that of a tennis court.
Breathing:

Breathing is simply the exchange of gases between your lungs and the air. It is a physical process that takes place at organism level. Lungs are spongy in nature and they cannot move on their own. The muscles surrounding the lungs expand or compress the lungs. When lungs expands air moves in (inhalation). When lungs compress the air moves out (exhalation).
Difference between Breathing and Respiration

Breathing | Respiration; It is a physical process involving exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide. | It is a biochemical process involving reaction of glucose with oxygen to produce carbon dioxide and water; Energy is not released | Energy is released; It takes place outside the cells | It takes place within the cells; Enzymes are not involved | Respiratory enzymes are involved

2.3 Circulatory System

Think about the cells in your toes. How do they get food and oxygen? How is the waste removed? Your blood transports all these substances. The system that moves blood throughout body is called the circulatory system. It includes the blood, blood vessels and the heart. The blood circulates in your body through a network of vessels and transports gases, nutrients, wastes and heat.
2.3 Circulatory System
Heart pumps this blood through your blood vessels.
Blood

The blood consists of plasma and blood cells. The plasma makes more than half of the volume of the blood. Plasma is a pale yellow coloured liquid. It carries water, nutrients, gases, wastes and chemicals (hormones, ions etc.) from one part of the body to another. Blood cells are of three types i.e. red blood cells, white blood cells and platelets.
Types of blood cells: Their structure, function and deficiency diseases

| Red blood cells | Platelets | White blood cells; Structure | Disc shaped with a depression on each side. Contain red haemoglobin | Irregular shaped, small pieces of cell | Different types, sizes and shapes; Function | Carry oxygen from lungs to rest of the body | Stop bleeding by forming clots | Protect your body from germs and harmful things.
Types of blood cells: Their structure, function and deficiency diseases

They make the immune system; Example of Deficiency Diseases | Anaemia due to less number of RBCs or haemoglobin quantity | Dengue fever virus reduces number of platelets | AIDS virus attacks WBCs and body immune system fails
Blood Vessels
Blood vessels can be thought of as highways your blood uses to move through your body. Your blood is always confined in blood vessels hence, it is called a closed circulatory system.
Blood Vessels

Arteries are blood vessels that carry blood away from the heart to other parts of your body. They have thick muscular walls that stretch when the heart pushes blood into artery. This stretching and thumping back produces pulse. Heart pushes blood into arteries with a pressure called blood pressure. Arteries carry oxygenated blood except pulmonary artery.
Blood Vessels

Arteries branch off into tiny vessels called capillaries. Capillaries are so narrow that RBCs flow through them in a single line. The walls of capillaries are only one cell thick so gases and small molecules can easily diffuse through these thin walls. Blood flow is slow in capillaries.
Blood Vessels

Capillaries join to form smallest veins. Veins are the blood vessels that take blood from cells back to the heart. The small veins join to form larger veins. Veins have thinner walls than the arteries. Veins have valves to avoid backward flow of blood.
Teaching Point

Interesting Facts

Your blood vessels are very long. If all your blood vessels are laid end to end, they would stretch around earth more than twice • Your blood sample is taken from veins as they are larger, have thinner walls and blood flow is slower in them

2.4 Heart

The heart is divided into two sides. Each side of the heart has two parts. The upper, blood receiving part of each side is called an atrium. The lower, blood distributing part is called a ventricle. Ventricles are larger, thicker walled and more powerful than atrium. The right side gets deoxygenated blood from the veins of the body and pumps it to lungs.
2.4 Heart

In the lungs, the blood gets oxygen and gives up carbon dioxide. This oxygenated blood flows to left side of the heart. The left side pumps this oxygenated blood through arteries to the body. Heart also has valves to keep blood flowing in one direction.

3.1 Immunity
Your body has a powerful army that protects it from various types of threats including:
3.1 Immunity
Mechanical injuries e.g., cuts, wounds etc. • Attack by pathogens • Entry of foreign particles like dust and pollen
Do You Know?

Pathogens are disease causing germs including virus, bacteria, fungi and parasites. Infectious diseases are diseases caused by these pathogens e.g., Flu caused by virus, Typhoid caused by bacteria etc.
3.1 Immunity

This personal army is called immune system. Every day we encounter a huge number of pathogens. However, we do not fall ill every other day which is due to our immune system. An army of cells is always roaming our body ready to ward off any attack. Immunity is the ability of the body to resist harmful microorganisms. There are three types of immunity i.e. innate, adaptive and passive immunity.
3.2 Innate Immunity

Innate immunity or nonspecific immunity is the natural defence of body against any intruder. This immunity acts without recognizing and differentiating the intruder. It has two components i.e., first line of defence and second line of defence.
3.2 Innate Immunity

First line of defence stops entry of germs in the body. It includes skin and mucus membranes of mouth, nose, lungs etc. • Second line of defence includes some white blood cells, chemicals and fever. These act after germs enter into body. All these factors kill germs and protect the body.
Do You Know?

There are ways to support your first line of defence. You can add layers of defence to protect your body like face mask, gloves, sanitizer etc. Can you think of some other ways to add additional layers of defence?
3.3 Adaptive Immunity
Adaptive immunity or learned immunity includes the third line of defence. It identifies the germ and start making special types of white blood cells i.e., T cells and B cells.
3.3 Adaptive Immunity

T cells directly kill virus infected cells and activate all other cells of immune system to fight the germs. B cells after activation start making antibodies. Antibodies are special proteins flowing in blood which can recognize and kill viruses and bacteria. If our body develops antibodies against a disease, then we become immune to that disease.
3.3 Adaptive Immunity
The way the body defends itself against harmful or foreign substances is called immune response.
3.4 Mechanism of Antibody Formation

There are two ways to start antibody formation by your immune system. Either you get disease or you get vaccination. Your immune system requires exposure of pathogen to activate and start antibody formation. A vaccine works by training the immune system to recognize and fight pathogens. To do this some part from the pathogen must be introduced into the body to trigger an immune response.
3.4 Mechanism of Antibody Formation
Vaccine can be in the form of oral drops e.g., Polio vaccine or injection e.g., Covid-19 vaccine.
3.4 Mechanism of Antibody Formation

B and T cells form memory cells as well. These memory cells remember their enemies. Next time when the pathogen enters these two types of memory cells become active immediately and start killing pathogens. This quick immune response assures that pathogen will be unable to grow in the body and cause disease.
3.4 Mechanism of Antibody Formation
So if you are vaccinated against Polio, then after the entry of Polio virus in your body your immune response will kill all Polio viruses. You will stay healthy and protected from diseases.
Teaching Point
Every one has first and second line of defence by birth. Third line of defence grows with time due to vaccine and exposure of pathogens.

3.5 Passive Immunity

Sometimes a pathogen or toxin harms body very quickly and immune system cannot protect the body. In such situation already prepared antibodies can save a person's life; Like after a snake bite, a person's life is threatened. Already prepared antibodies are injected which stop the effect of snake venom. This type of immunity is short lived and it is called passive immunity.
Do You Know?

You get passive immunity naturally from your mother. Before birth, antibodies are passed through the placenta to protect the child from illness. After birth, an infant receives antibodies found in mother's breast milk. It is also called maternal passive immunity.
3.6 Ways to Boost Your Immunity

Eat lots of fruits and vegetables. • Drink plenty of water. • Exercise regularly and maintain healthy weight. • Get a good night's sleep. • Stay hopeful, happy and connected with family and friends. • Wash your hands more often and keep yourself clean. • Avoid fried foods, sugar, smoking, drugs etc. • Get recommended vaccination.

Physical and Chemical Changes

Many activities take place around us where we can observe matter changing into other forms. Sometimes the changes can be reversed while sometimes the changes cannot be reversed. Do you think the burning of wood can be reversed?
Physical and Chemical Changes
There exist two types of changes in matter 1) Physical Changes 2) Chemical Changes
4.1 Physical Changes

Chopping of wood and melting of ice are examples of physical changes. In physical changes, no new substances are formed. When ice melts it changes its form from solid ice to liquid water which can be reversed by putting it back in a freezer. Similarly, when the wood is chopped, it is broken into smaller pieces and each piece is still wood. No new change has occurred.
4.1 Physical Changes
Cutting, tearing, grinding, shredding and mixing are examples of physical change because they change the form but not the composition of a material.

4.2 Chemical Changes

Chemical changes take place only when matter changes to become an entirely different kind of matter. For example, when we burn wood it changes into two new substances: black smoke (gas) and ashes. Burning is also called combustion.
4.2 Chemical Changes
Formation of yoghurt and making of food by plant in the process of respiration are also examples of chemical change.
Interesting Facts
Always remember: A new substance is always formed in a chemical reaction, because, the particles in the matter can be rearranged however, the mass of the matter will always remain the same.
Interesting Facts

Antoine Lavoisier was the scientist who recognised the discovery of the law of conservation of mass. This law states that "In a chemical reaction, the matter is neither destroyed nor created but it may be changed from one form to another."

Describe and draw the structure of an atom in terms of electrons, protons and neutrons. • Describe how an atom is electrically neutral. • Differentiate between atomic number and mass number. • Determine the atomic number and mass number of elements based on the number of protons, electrons and neutrons. • Show the arrangement of electrons in K, L and M shells of elements.

• Draw the atomic structure of the first eighteen elements of the periodic table. • Explain that the periodic table is a way to organize elements systematically. • Recognize groups and periods in the periodic table.
Structure of an Atom
Let's see if you remember, what is a matter made of? Can you see an atom? Which is smaller; an atom or a molecule?
Structure of an Atom

The matter is made of tiny particles called atoms. Just as a wall is made of small bricks, living organisms consist of cells and honeycomb is made up of smaller hexagonal cells. Element is a pure matter which has the same type of atoms and retains all of the chemical properties of that element. For example, a gold coin is made up of gold atoms put together in a shape of a coin.
5.1 Structure of an Atom

An atom consists of two regions as shown in the diagram in the figure 5.1. The centre of the atom is called a nucleus. The nucleus contains protons and neutrons. Protons have a positive charge, whereas neutrons have no charge, means they are neutral. The second, much larger, region of the atom is a "cloud" of electrons. Electrons carry a negative charge and they orbit around the nucleus in fixed shells.
5.1 Structure of an Atom
Protons, neutrons and electrons are called subatomic particles.
5.1 Structure of an Atom
The number of protons and electrons of an atom is always the same which makes an atom a neutral entity.
Structure of an atom over the years

Model | Scientist | Year; Solid Sphere Model | John Dalton | 1803; Plum Pudding Model | J.J. Thomson | 1904; Nuclear Model | Ernest Rutherford | 1911; Planetary Model | Niels Bohr | 1913; Quantum Model | Erwin Schrödinger | 1926
Structure of an atom over the years

Atoms are present everywhere! From your car to your bicycle, a ladder, a chair, your cat and even your boots! They are tiny and cannot be seen with naked eye. Protons and neutrons form the centre of the nucleus!
5.2 Atomic Number

The number of proton(s) in an atom is called the proton number or atomic number and it is represented as Z. Atoms of different elements have different atomic numbers i.e., an element with 6 protons is a carbon atom, which means the atomic number of carbon is 6, similarly, the number of protons in oxygen is 8, therefore the proton number of oxygen is 8.
5.2 Atomic Number
In a modern periodic table, elements are arranged in order of increasing atomic numbers. The number of protons defines the identity of an element.
5.3 Mass Number

The number of protons and neutrons together is the mass number of an atom and it is represented with the letter A. Both protons and neutrons are also called nucleons. For example, an atom of carbon has 6 protons and 6 neutrons. Thus, its mass number is 12.
Modern periodic Table

Elements are arranged in increasing number of protons or we can say increasing atomic number. • Horizontal rows are also called periods that show the same number of shells for the elements. There are 7 periods in the periodic table. Elements like Hydrogen and Helium are in Period-1 which mean they have one orbit of the electron.
Modern periodic Table

Elements such as Sodium and Magnesium, Aluminium, are in Period-3 meaning they have three electron orbits. • Vertical columns are also called groups, there are 18 groups and they have different properties. For example, Group 18 has the noble gases – Helium, Neon, Argon, Radon, Krypton and Xenon which have low melting and boiling points, and they each are colourless, odourless, tasteless, and non-flammable.
Modern periodic Table
This group is called as low chemical reactive group.
Modern periodic Table
Distribution of metals and non-metals in the periodic table is shown in figure 5.4:
Finding the Number of Protons

The number of protons in an atom is equal to the atomic number of the element. For example according to the periodic table, oxygen has the atomic number eight. The atomic number is placed above the element's symbol. It means it has eight protons.
Finding the Number of Neutrons

The number of neutrons in an atom can be calculated by subtracting the atomic number from the atomic mass. Both of these numbers can be found in the periodic table. The atomic number is listed above the symbol of the element whereas the mass number is placed below.
Finding the Number of Electrons

The number of electrons in an atom is equal to the atomic number of an element. The number of electrons and the number of protons in an element are equal. Therefore, the number of electrons in oxygen is 8. These subatomic particles, electrons and protons, have opposite charges, they cancel out and keep the atom neutral.
5.4 Distribution of Electrons in Shells
Electrons move around the nucleus in fixed shells named K, L, M and so on. The maximum number of electrons a shell can hold is given by the formula 2n², where n is the shell number.
5.4 Distribution of Electrons in Shells
K shell (n = 1): 2 × 1² = 2 electrons • L shell (n = 2): 2 × 2² = 8 electrons • M shell (n = 3): 2 × 3² = 18 electrons

Do You Know?

Atoms of noble gases are less reactive and stable due to their complete outermost shells. The maximum number of electrons filled in the first shell is two. This is called the duplet. Helium has a duplet. • The maximum number of electrons which can be filled in the second shell is eight. This is called octet. Neon (Atomic number = 10) has eight electrons in its outermost shell and has a complete octet.
Key Points

An atom is made up of three subatomic particles: protons, electrons and neutrons. • An atom is electrically neutral. This means that in an atom the number of protons is equal to the number of electrons. • Mass number of an element is the sum of the number of protons and the number of neutrons present in the nucleus. • Atomic number is the number of protons in an atom.
Key Points
• The distribution of electrons in their shells is called the electronic configuration.

At the end of this unit, students will be able to:
Learning outcomes:

Define valency and explain the formation of ions. • Write chemical formulae on the basis of valency of the constituent elements such as H₂O, NaCl, NH₃, CO₂, CO, etc. • Recognize that a chemical bond results from the attraction between atoms in a compound and that the atoms' electrons are involved in this bonding.
6.1 Valency
Have you ever thought why do elements combine?
6.1 Valency

Elements combine to form bonds. The combining capacity of the atom to form a chemical bond is called its valency. The valency of an element is the number of electrons its atom gains, loses or shares, to form a compound. Valency is always in small whole numbers or zero. The elements which have zero valency do not form compounds.
6.1 Valency
Look at the table and observe how compounds are formed by using valency.
6.1 Valency
Elements | No. of valence electrons | In forming a compound, the atom...
6.1 Valency

| The valency of the element; Group I | 1 | Loses 1 electron | 1; Group II | 2 | Loses 2 electrons | 2; Group III | 3 | Loses 3 electrons | 3; Group IV | 4 | Shares 4 electrons | 4; Group V | 5 | Gains or shares 3 electrons | 3; Group VI | 6 | Gains or shares 2 electrons | 2; Group VII | 7 | Gains or shares 1 electron | 1; Group 0 | 8 | Rarely form compounds, least reactive | Zero
6.2 Formation of Ions
You have studied that an atom loses or gains one or more electrons to form a compound.
6.2 Formation of Ions
An atom is a neutral particle. But, when an electron is added or removed from an atom, it becomes a charged particle known as an ion.
6.2 Formation of Ions
An ion is a charged particle formed either by loss or gain of one or more electrons.
Formation of Cations (Losing electrons)
Sodium metal loses an electron and becomes a positively charged ion called "cation".
Formation of Cations (Losing electrons)

Chlorine gains an electron and becomes a negatively charged ion called "anion".

6.3 Chemical Formula

Every compound has a chemical formula. For example, the compound of sodium and chlorine is called sodium chloride. Chemical formula can also be determined by using the valency of an atom. The chemical formula is a symbolic representation of the elements that are bonded together in a compound. Chemical formula is used to describe the types of atoms and their numbers present in a compound / molecule.
Steps for writing chemical formula

1. Write down the symbols of the elements. • 2. Above each symbol write its valency. • 3. Cross the valency of both elements. • 4. If the valency can be simplified, divide them by the least valency. • 5. Write the chemical formula.
How to write chemical formula

Compound | Groups | Crossing valencies | Formula; 1. Sodium chloride | Na: Group IA; Cl: Group VII A | Na¹ ✕ Cl¹ | NaCl; 2. Water | H: Group IA; O: Group VI A | H¹ ✕ O² | H₂O; 3. Ammonia | N: Group VA; H: Group IA | N³ ✕ H¹ | NH₃; 4. Carbon dioxide | C: Group IVA; O: Group VI A | C⁴ ✕ O² → C₂O₄ | CO₂
6.4 Chemical Bond

A chemical bond is a mutual attraction between the nuclei and valence electrons of different atoms that binds the atoms together. The valence electrons are involved in bonding of one atom to another. The attraction of each atom's nucleus for the valence electrons of the other atom pulls the atoms together.
6.4 Chemical Bond

When two atoms interact with each other, they experience a force of attraction. Electrons have a negative charge and the nuclei have positive charge. The nucleus of one atom attracts the electrons of the other atom. When atoms come close to each other both attractive and repulsive forces increase as the distance between the atoms decreases. This electrostatic attraction holds the two atoms together.
6.4 Chemical Bond
As the attraction brings the atoms together, electrons from each atom are attracted to the nucleus of both atoms and form chemical bonds.
Key Points

Valency is the combining capacity of atoms to form bonds. • The chemical formula is the symbolic representation of the elements that are bonded together in a compound. • Chemical formula can also be determined by using the valency of an atom. • A chemical bond is a mutual force of attraction between atoms that causes them to come together in a specific pattern to form a compound.
