5.4.1 Hacking

Hacking is an unauthorized attempt to gain access to someone's computer or network. The person engaged in hacking activities is known as hacker. A hacker may alter system or security features such as password, to accomplish a goal that differs from the original purpose of the system. It also aims to have access to important data and information, breaching privacy.
5.4.2 Identity Theft

Identity theft is a specific form of fraud in which cybercriminals steal personal information and data. These may include passwords, data about the bank account, credit cards, debit cards, social security, and other sensitive information. Through identity theft, criminals can steal money and obtain other benefits in other person's name.
5.4.3 Cyber bullying

Cyber bullying or Cyber harassment is an online act of threatening people. The harmful bullying behavior can include posting rumors, threats, personal remarks, sharing victims' personal information or hate speech etc. Cyber bullying can take place on social media sites such as Facebook, MSN or Twitter etc.
5.4.4 Malicious Software

Malicious Software, commonly known as Malware, is a program which causes harms to a computer or network in the form of viruses, worms, trojans, spyware, adware etc. Common symptoms of malware attacks include automatic rebooting of computer, computer running slow, deletion of files, etc.
5.4.5 Computer Viruses

A computer virus is a malicious program that are designed to spread from device to device and are attached with other files and documents. In other words, the computer virus spreads by itself into other executable code or documents. The purpose of creating a computer virus is to infect vulnerable systems, gain admin control and steal user sensitive data.
5.4.5 Computer Viruses

One of the ideal methods by which viruses spread is through emails – opening the attachment in the email, visiting an infected website, clicking on an executable file, or viewing an infected advertisement can cause the virus to spread to your system. Besides that, infections also spread while connecting with already infected removable storage devices such as USB drives.
5.4.6 Protection Against Malware
Keep Windows and other software updated. • Install antivirus software and keep it updated. • Frequently scan your computer for malware to remove it with antivirus software.
5.4.6 Protection Against Malware
Be careful when downloading email attachments as these may be infected with malware. • Download material only from trusted website.
5.4.7 Financial Fraud

Financial frauds often occur when someone releases his bank account information to the offender or through some response to an email or on phone call soliciting account details. This may include the identity theft of a victim. The offender then uses the victims personal information to create additional accounts through which money is laundered, or to open additional credit cards etc.
5.4.8 Cyberstalking

Cyber stalking refers to the use of the Internet or other electronic means to harass an individual, group, or organization. It may include false accusations, defamation and identity theft for harassment.
5.4.9 Money Laundering

Money laundering is the process of making transaction to hide actual source of money. The rise of online banking system, online payment services, and money transfers using mobile phones, have made detecting the illegal transfer of money more difficult. Money can also be laundered through online auctions and sales, gambling websites and even virtual gaming sites.

Electronic or Cyber terrorism is the use of Internet to conduct violent acts that result in or threaten, loss of life or significant bodily harm to the victim. The activities may include acts of disrupting on large scale computer networks by transmitting computer viruses, computer worms and or installing unwanted software or programming scripts etc.
5.4.11 Vandalism and Extortion

Computer vandalism is a process where in there is a program that performs malicious function like extracting user's password or other data and/or erasing the hard disk. 6.2 Design Thinking
Design thinking is a process for creative problem solving which leads to better products and internal processes.
6.2 Design Thinking
Design thinking is an iterative process that teams use to understand user's requirement, redefine problems and create innovative solutions to prototype and test.
6.2 Design Thinking

Design Thinking is extremely useful in tackling problems that are ill-defined or unknown, by reframing the problem in human-centric ways, creating many ideas in brainstorm sessions, and adopting a hands-on approach in prototyping and testing. Design Thinking also involves ongoing experimentation like sketching, prototyping, testing, and trying out concepts and ideas.
6.2.1 Stages of Design Thinking

The following are the stages of the Design thinking process: Empathize → Define → Ideate → Prototype → Test. These stages are not always sequential and teams often run them in parallel, out of order and repeat them in an iterative fashion.
Stage 1: Empathize

Empathize is the first stage of the design thinking process. One of the main objective of Empathize stage is to identify user needs and behaviors. Design teams conduct research to know the exact requirement of the user. They try to get insights of the user by observing and consulting with them. This way, they can understand users' experiences, motivations and problems.
Stage 1: Empathize
Organizations can motivate creativity and innovation by solving such problems using technology.
Stage 1: Empathize

In a social context, empathy is often what drives us to take action. If we see people suffering or struggling, and we are able to empathize with their situation, we are compelled to help relieve them in some way.
Stage 1: Empathize
Designers need to build empathy for their users in order to take the right course of action. It is very important to understand the feeling of user while talking about the product or interface.
Stage 1: Empathize

In building empathy, designers can create products which truly please the user and make their lives easier. Without this empathy, the design process lacks the actual need of the end user which often marks the distinction between product success and failure.
Stage 2: Define

Information gathered during the Empathize stage is further analyzed to define the core problems identified in above mentioned stage. These definitions are called problem statement. You can create roles to keep your efforts human-centered before proceeding to ideation.
Stage 3: Ideate

The outcomes of the two previous stages (e.g. Empathize and Define) enables a designer to generate ideas and think outside the box. In this stage, a designer comes up with new ideas and identifies innovative solutions to the problem.
Stage 4: Prototype

This is an experimental phase. The main objective of this stage is to identify the best possible solution for each problem found. A designer must produce some inexpensive, scaled-down versions of the product to shape the ideas generated in the previous stage. This could involve simply paper prototyping.
Stage 5: Test

Finally, the prototypes are evaluated using different evaluators to test whether the prototype is producing the desired output or not. Design Thinking is an iterative process, teams may use the results to redefine one or more further problems. Hence, you can return to previous stages to make further iterations, alterations and refinements to find out alternative solutions.

1.1 Processes Responsible for Change in Landscape of the Earth

Landforms are the natural features that make up the earth's surface. These natural features have different profile and relief, therefore there exist a vast variety of landforms. The major landforms on the surface of the earth are plains, plateaus and mountains. These landforms are widespread on the face of the Earth. All of us interact with some or all of these at a time.
1.1 Processes Responsible for Change in Landscape of the Earth
There are two types of processes of the Earth, one develops many patterns and landscapes and other changes these landscapes.
1.1 Processes Responsible for Change in Landscape of the Earth
Diastrophism, volcanoes, folding and faulting, originate in the interior of the earth and create mountain ranges, oceanic ridges, trenches and rift valleys.
1.1 Processes Responsible for Change in Landscape of the Earth

Other set of earth processes continuously evolve surface of the Earth. These are weathering, erosion, and mass movement. They affect the surface of the earth and change the structure of landforms to other types of landforms. These processes erode, transport and deposit materials. Resultantly over long period of time, large mountains turns into small hills, and finally, these are turned to plains.
1.1 Processes Responsible for Change in Landscape of the Earth
A brief introduction of these processes is as under.
1.1 Processes Responsible for Change in Landscape of the Earth
i) Weathering is breaking down of rocks of the surface of the earth by Mechanical or Chemical means.
a) Mechanical Weathering

Mechanical weathering breaks the rock without changing their composition. Weathering by mechanical means involves processes like freezing and thawing of water, expansion and contraction of rocks and wedging by plant roots.
b) Chemical Weathering

Chemical weathering occurs when minerals of rocks react with water and gases of the earth's atmosphere. It produces new weaker substances by changing the composition of the minerals of rocks. New weaker substances formed so, change the physical appearance of the rocks. The chemical weathering occurs through carbonation, oxidation and hydrolysis.
b) Chemical Weathering

ii) Mass wasting is the movement of a large mass of sediments or a section of land, down a slope due to gravity. There are different types of mass wasting such as rock fall, landslide, avalanches, creep and mudflow.
b) Chemical Weathering

iii) Erosion is the wearing and removal of land surface by rivers, winds and glaciers. Erosional processes evolve the landforms in terms of elevation, shape and size. These agents pile up their materials in a process called deposition that results in formation of new landforms.
b) Chemical Weathering
Rivers, winds and glaciers not only erode the respective land surfaces but they also carry eroded material down through transportation process.

1.3 Plains

Rivers, glaciers, and winds are major agents of change working on the surface of the earth. These agents have developed following types of plains through erosional and depositional processes. Erosion is the wearing away and removal of exposed land by river, wind and glacier. Depositional process is the accumulation of load carried by these agents.
1.3 Plains

i. Erosional Plains: When a mountain or plateau area is reduced to a low lying plain by weathering and erosion over a very long period of time, an erosional plain is formed which is termed as peneplain. The plains of Northern Europe and Northern Canada are erosional plains.
1.3 Plains
ii. Depositional Plains: These are formed by the deposition of sediments on lowlands, brought by rivers, glaciers or the wind.
1.4 Features of River Plains

a. River Plains: The largest depositional plains are formed by the deposition of sediments by rivers. They are also termed as alluvial, flood or deltaic plains. Such plains are ideal for farming as they are flat and fertile. The Indus Plains in Pakistan are depositional Plains formed by the River Indus and its tributaries.
1.4 Features of River Plains
b. Outwash / Till Plains: Glaciers also spread sediments of various sizes to form outwash or till plains. They are located in Northern Germany and MidWest of U.S.A.
1.4 Features of River Plains
c. Loess Plains: Loess plains are formed by deposition of very fine particles by wind known as loess. Winds blew these particles from deserts. The Pampas of Argentina are loess covered plains.
1.4 Features of River Plains

iii. Coastal Plains: These plains were formed when a part of the sea floor bordering a continent was uplifted. They occur in Scotland and along the South-East coast of the U.S.A. In Pakistan coastal plains are located along Sindh and Makran coast.
1.4 Features of River Plains

iv. Structural Plains: They are formed by horizontally bedded rocks, relatively undisturbed by the tectonic activities of the earth. They include the Russian platform, the great plains of U.S.A and the central lowlands of Australia.
1.4 Features of River Plains

We know that plains are flat or gently rolling land surfaces. As we know that Rivers are among the major agents of change and play a key role in shaping the landscape of the earth. In plains they develop a variety of features out of which, following features are very common.
1.4 Features of River Plains

River Braiding: Bars of sediments accumulate in the course of the river and these bars divide the river into several channels. These channels converge and get separated again by bars. This split of a river into several channels, that alternately converge and get separated is termed as river braiding.
1.4 Features of River Plains

Meanders: Meanders are loop-like bends present in the plains. Meanders become bigger because of sluggish flow of water, and sometimes two bends of a meander may come close to each other and form the neck of the meander. In case the river cuts through the neck of the meander to flow straight, the cut-off loop becomes separated and forms an ox-bow lake.
1.4 Features of River Plains

Flood Plains: In times of heavy rainfall, the river overflows its banks, this phenomenon is called flooding. The overflowing water spreads over the land adjacent to both banks of the river and there it deposits sand, silt, and clay. This deposition results in the formation of the flood plains over time.
1.4 Features of River Plains

Levees: A river flow is fastest in the middle of the river and its speed is slowest at the sides along the river banks. This slow flowage of river water along its banks causes the dropping of much of the sand, silt and clay by its sides. This dropped material forms natural embankments called levees.

1.6 Stages of a River Course

The whole length of the river is termed as its course. The course of a river has three distinct stages. This includes the upper course, the middle course, and the lower course. They have different land features, that are formed by the erosional and depositional work of the river.
i) The Upper Course
The upper course of a river is also called the youth stage. This is the mountainous stage of the river. River forms several features in its upper course e.g. valleys, waterfalls, and gorges.
i) The Upper Course

In this stage the speed of the river water is fast as it flows on steep slopes. The river carries stones, boulders, and particles as its load. The river erodes its bed downwards with the help of its load, carving out V-shaped valleys. These valleys are narrow, deep and steep.
i) The Upper Course

When the river flows from hard to soft rocks, the soft rocks are eroded away, leaving behind overhanging hard rocks. The river plunges down as a waterfall from the overhanging hard rocks. Niagara Falls in North America is one of the most famous waterfalls. Basin shaped land features, termed as plunge pools, are formed under waterfalls by the natural force of falling water.
ii) The Middle Course

The middle course of a river is called its mature stage. In the mature stage river water loses its speed and force as it is flowing in a plain area. It can only carry light and small particles of rocks and it begins to deposit its heavy loads. A River takes winding courses in this stage; many tributaries join it, resulting an increase in its volume.
iii) The Lower Course
The lower course of a river is called its old stage. The river flows in a flat and very wide valley. River flow is slow. Major work of the river is to deposit its load over flat and wide valley.
iii) The Lower Course

When a river enters a sea, it drops its material at the river mouth resulting in a large triangular landform called a delta. The Nile, Indus and Hwang-Ho rivers have triangular deltas. The Nile Delta spreads out across 150 miles (240 km) of the Egyptian coast on the Mediterranean Sea.

2.1 Water Sources of the World and Pakistan
Water is an essential part of human life, as it is used for different activities such as drinking, washing, cleaning, agriculture, industry, power generation, and construction.
2.1 Water Sources of the World and Pakistan
There are numerous sources of water on the Earth, ranging from surface sources to underground sources.
A. Water Sources of the World

i. Oceans: Oceans are the biggest source of water on the Earth. The five oceans of the world i.e. Pacific Ocean, Atlantic Ocean, Indian Ocean, Arctic Ocean and the Southern/Antarctic Ocean, contain approximately 97% of all the water on the planet.
A. Water Sources of the World

ii. Lakes: Lakes are sources of surface-water. Water from precipitation or rivers accumulate in depressions on the Earth's surface to form lakes. Sometimes, lakes form in area where groundwater seeps up to the surface to form a lake. This activity takes place in areas where water table lies at less depth. Lakes contain 0.008% of all the water on the planet.
A. Water Sources of the World

iii. Rivers: Rivers or streams are the natural pathways of rainwater and melted water flowing across the surface of the Earth from higher to lower elevations. They discharge their water in oceans, seas and lakes. Rivers contain 0.0002% of all the water on the planet.
A. Water Sources of the World
iv. Aquifers: Aquifers are subsurface sources of the water. Aquifers contain 0.9% of all the water on the planet.

A. Water Sources of the World

v. Glaciers and Ice Caps: Glaciers and ice caps are fresh water sources in frozen form. They are formed when snow accumulates over land areas for long period of time. They are found in regions of high elevation and areas close to the North and South poles, and they store more than a third of the earth's fresh water. Glaciers and ice caps contain about 2% of all the water on the planet.
A. Water Sources of the World

vi. Rainfall: Rainfall is one of the most important sources of water for agriculture in arid region. It is seasonal in nature. Two-thirds of all rain falls along the equator while the rest of the world gets only one third.

vii. Springs: Springs are naturally occurring freshwater sources found in those places where the water table is located close to the earth's surface. They obtain their water either from aquifers or from underground streams. Springs located in regions of volcanoes have hot water, while springs found in area where no volcanic activity takes place produce cold water.
A. Water Sources of the World

viii. Ponds: Ponds are surface water sources that are mostly smaller than lakes. Some ponds occur naturally while others are man-made. The main source of water for naturally occurring ponds is rainfall. Pond water is often used for irrigation, fishing and landscaping.

What's the difference between rain, sleet and snow? When the air is sufficiently saturated, water vapour begins to form clouds. If saturation continues, water droplets grow and merge to fall as rain. Snow forms when the air is cold enough to freeze water droplets. Sleet is somewhere in between.
B. Water Sources of Pakistan

i. Rivers: The river Indus and its eastern and western tributaries are the main sources of water in Pakistan. The Indus river basin comprises the Indus river and its major tributaries (Kabul, Jhelum, Chenab, Ravi and Sutlej rivers). Approximately 50 to 80% of the total average river flows in the Indus river system are fed by snow and glaciers, while the remainder are fed from monsoon rains.
B. Water Sources of Pakistan

Although most of the Indus river basin is located in a region of deficient rainfall with less than 10 inches of annual precipitation, heavy rains during the monsoon season account for more than 50% of its annual flow.
B. Water Sources of Pakistan

ii. Rain: Rain is an important source of water in Pakistan. Only a small part of it receives rainfall in excess of 1000 mm. This includes: Murree, Hazara and Swat etc. Upper Indus plain, Astore, Chitral, Bannu, Peshawar, Zhob and Quetta etc., receive rainfall in range of 250 to 1000 mm, whereas the rest of Pakistan receives less than 250 mm of rain annually.
B. Water Sources of Pakistan

iii. Glaciers: There are more than 5,000 glaciers having a surface area of about 20,000 Km² in the catchment of the Upper Indus River basin. These glaciers serve as the source of meltwater flowing into the Indus river and its tributaries.
B. Water Sources of Pakistan

iv. Dams: These have been built on Indus river and its tributaries for storing water. Large dams like Tarbela and Mangla are multi-purpose projects that store water and supply it for irrigation, power generation, recreation and human consumption, whereas smaller dams like the Rawal Dam, Khanpur Dam and Hub Dam are used to store and supply water for agriculture and domestic use.

Hundreds of natural lakes exist in Pakistan. Most of these are located in the mountainous regions but many are located in the plain areas. Among these, the Manchar lake is a famous large freshwater lake in Sindh province.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan

The water that is found underground in sand and rocks is termed as groundwater. It is stored underground as aquifers. It supplies water for human consumption and agricultural uses. Groundwater pumping fulfils these purposes and results in lowering of ground water level. Many areas of Pakistan are experiencing low groundwater table.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan
It plays a pivotal role in mitigating the impacts of less water availability through canal water supply and rainfall.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan
The main reasons behind lowering of ground water levels are:
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan

i. Increase in cultivated areas irrigated by groundwater: As the area under agriculture increases, the demand for water also increases. As a result, farmers start using groundwater for irrigation and its continuous use leads to lowering of the ground water table.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan

ii. Water-intensive irrigation: Pumping groundwater at a rate faster than its rate of recharge can have negative effects on the level of groundwater. Water-intensive irrigation practice lead to stress on surface water irrigation resources, forcing farmers to pump groundwater for irrigation purposes. This practice results in lowering of ground water.
Do you know?
Irrigation is an agricultural process in which controlled amount of water is applied to crops. There are different means of irrigation such as tube well, karez and canals etc.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan

iii. Reduced rainfall: Low rainfall is major contributor to groundwater lowering through depletion. The most important source for the recharge of groundwater is the infiltration and percolation of rainwater through soil. When rainfall is reduced due to climate change, the seepage of rainwater through the ground also reduces and results in a lowering of the water table.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan

iv. Deforestation and removal of vegetation: In absence of vegetation cover, falling of rain drops onto the ground results in fast flow/runoff across the ground surface. Fast runoff does not allow much time for the water to seep into the ground.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan
Presence of vegetation retards the rapid falling of rain drops, resulting rainwater reaches the ground slowly and results in more seepage and less runoff and ground water is recharged.
2.2 Reasons for Low Groundwater in Pakistan

vi. Rapid urbanization: Rapid urbanization leads to greater use of groundwater for domestic and commercial purposes. Moreover urbanized areas are covered by buildings and roads and very little bare ground is left. Bare ground is necessary for the recharge of groundwater by rainfall. Rainwater cannot penetrate concrete and asphalt to recharge the ground water.
Do you know?

Urbanization is the transformation of sparsely occupied places into densely occupied cities. Urban areas can grow in case of an increase in human population or due to migration from rural to urban areas.
2.3 The Scarcity of Drinking Water in Cities
The rapid urbanization that has been taking place in developing countries for the past few decades has created many problems for the people living in cities.
2.3 The Scarcity of Drinking Water in Cities
One of these problems is the scarcity of water. Most of the larger cities in the developing world are facing this problem. The main reasons behind this problem are:
2.3 The Scarcity of Drinking Water in Cities
i). Climate change is causing decreased rainfall across many regions of the world and a reduction in rainfall means a reduction in the fresh water resources available for drinking.
2.3 The Scarcity of Drinking Water in Cities

ii). The ground surface of urban areas are invariably covered with concrete buildings and asphalt roads. This leaves very little bare ground to absorb rainwater, and without much rainwater absorption/seepage it becomes very difficult to recharge groundwater. When groundwater is not recharged, the water table begins to fall and people have a hard time accessing it for domestic use.
2.3 The Scarcity of Drinking Water in Cities

iii). Lack of proper city planning is also a cause of water scarcity in cities. In Pakistan, most of the existing cities are unplanned and their rapidly expanding population does not have access to water for domestic use.

2.5 Water Cycle
Water Cycle, powered by solar heat energy is constantly transforming and transporting water around the Earth, to maintain the water supply of the Earth.

High earth surface temperatures cause evaporation from surface water sources like oceans, seas, rivers and lakes. The resulting water vapour rises in the atmosphere alongwith the air, until it encounters cooler temperatures. These cooler temperatures cause the transformation of water vapor into clouds due to the process of condensation. Clouds results in precipitation in the form of rain, snow and hail.

This precipitation adds water back into the oceans, lakes, rivers, and groundwater reserves.

2.6 Sewage Waste

Sewage is a mixture of both domestic and industrial wastes. It is a major carrier of disease and toxins. Waste water can originate from both industrial and domestic sources. It contains water, suspended solids and harmful bacteria that must be removed before the water is released into streams.
2.6 Sewage Waste

a. Uses of Sewage waste: Sewage waste can be used as an irrigation source due to high organic content and plant nutrients. It enhances crop productivity. In suburban areas, farmers usually use sewage waste to grow vegetables and fodder. They earn many times higher income through this practice.
2.6 Sewage Waste

Sewage must be treated before applying to the fields, as it is rich in high pathogen load, heavy metals and organic pollutants. The safe treatment of sewage is thus crucial to the health of any community.
b. Methods of Sewage Treatment
The basic methods of sewage treatment are:
b. Methods of Sewage Treatment

i. Physical Method: Physical Method is basically the process of removing small and large floating and suspended solids from sewage through the processes of screening, filtration and sedimentation. Screening removes paper, wood and other large items. Filtration removes suspended particles or floating particles. The filtered water is then kept in large open tanks where the suspended impurities settle down.
b. Methods of Sewage Treatment
ii. Biological Method: Biological Method which is the treatment of human waste by bacteria and micro-organisms that convert the sewage waste into by products such as sludge.
b. Methods of Sewage Treatment
iii. Chemical Method: In a chemical method, chemicals are used to treat waste water. For example, chlorine and ozone are used to eliminate germs and bacteria.

2.7 Biogas as a Resource of Energy

Biological treatment of sewage can produce useful gases such as biogas that can be used as energy sources. The method used for this purpose is called "anaerobic digestion" and the equipment used for this purpose is called an "anaerobic digester". Sewage is pumped into anaerobic digestion tanks where anaerobic bacteria break it down in the absence of oxygen.
2.7 Biogas as a Resource of Energy
One of the main by-products of this process is biogas, which is then collected from the anaerobic digestion tanks with the help of equipment called biogas recovery units.
2.7 Biogas as a Resource of Energy

The main disadvantage of biogas is that when it used as a fuel, methane gas is released into the atmosphere and since it is one of the most potent greenhouse gas, it can greatly contribute to global warming.

Following are some of the common water purification methods.
2.8 Water Purification Methods

Through condensation, the water vapours become liquid water and are collected as purified water and the heavier contaminants stay behind in the original container.

ii. Reverse Osmosis: Reverse osmosis is a purification process that utilizes a semi-permeable membrane. Pumps are used to push the impure water into the membrane that blocks most of the impurities while letting purified water go through to the other side.

3.1 Suitable Conditions for a Settlement

A Settlement is a place where people dwell, live together and carry out their social and economic activities. Human settlements can be a temporary dwelling or permanent place to live in. They include Huts, hamlets, villages, towns and mega cities.
Fertile Crescent

The Fertile Crescent is a semicircular area of the Eastern Mediterranean region, including the valleys of Nile, Tigris and Euphrates River. It is also known as "Cradle of civilization" because it is believed that some of the most ancient human settlements come from this region. Indus valley is also one of the earliest civilizations.
3.1 Suitable Conditions for a Settlement

The location and a growth of a settlement depends upon on its site and situation. The site is actual land where people decide to build settlement. The situation can be defined as the location of a place in relation to its surroundings. The situation of a settlement is the most important for its future and growth.
3.1 Suitable Conditions for a Settlement

Situation involves many factors such as physical features (mountains, rivers, sea coast) economic activity (agriculture, mining, industry), transportation routes, (roads, railways, sea port). Location is often mentioned with reference to longitude and latitude. In daily use, it is measured as a distance and direction from a known point.
3.1 Suitable Conditions for a Settlement

Geographers often study the factors that lead settlement towards becoming a large city over time or remaining as a small village. Favourable factors that influence the location of a settlement include:
1. Food and Water Supply

Water is the basic need of life. Settlements are therefore located near a source of water like rivers. Rivers provide constant supply of water for drinking and agricultural purposes. That is why we find large number of settlements in river valleys. Many of the main cities and towns of the world are built around rivers. For example Lahore was built on river Ravi and London on River Thames.
2. Shelter and Defence

Early settlements were built on such landscape that could be a natural barrier to defend the city against enemies. Rome, Athens, and Jerusalem were built on hilltops because they were a natural barrier for the defence of the city. Similarly, an Island was preferred for settlement because it is difficult for others to reach, e.g. Durham is built inside a meander.
2. Shelter and Defence

Map conventions have made the understanding of very difficult Geography concepts easy. Now we can easily understand The International Date Line and Time zones by using the Map Conventions.
Time zones

Time zones are regions of the Earth that have same standard time, adjacent time zones are one hour apart from each other. There are 24 world time zones. The International Date Line

The International Date Line is located along 180° meridian. It is halfway around the world from the 0° Prime Meridian. Prime Meridian is the reference point of time zones, which runs through Greenwich, UK.
The International Date Line
The date line runs from the North Pole to the South Pole. It is not straight, it curves around landmasses and national borders to maintain the date of a landmass or a nation.
The International Date Line

Each calendar day starts from International Date Line. When a pesrson crosses the date line traveling east, he subtracts a day, and if he crosses the line traveling west, he adds a day. For example, Kiribati and Hawaii are on different sides of the date line. If we travel from Kiribati to Hawaii, we need to turn the clock back 22 hours, as Hawaii is 22 hours behind Kiribati.

Calculation of Hours

Earth is spherical in shape, there are 360° of longitudes. Earth takes 24 Hours to complete one rotation. It means 360° are covered in 24 hours. Therefore, in 1 hour, earth will rotate 15° (360° ÷ 24).
Calculation of Minutes
Earth completes one rotation in = 1440 minutes (24 x 60min) • Time difference between any two longitudes is 4 minutes (1440 ÷ 360)
Calculation of Minutes
Q. If it is 12 O'clock in Sialkot (Pakistan) located at 75° E. What would be the time in Riyadh (Saudi Arabia) located at 46° E.
Calculation of Minutes

Solution: Difference of longitudes between Sialkot and Riyadh 75° E - 46° E = 29° E. We know that time difference between any two longitudes is 4 minutes. Difference of time between 29° of longitudes = 29° x 4min = 116 minutes. (1 hour 56 minutes) Riyadh is located in west of Pakistan, 1 hours 56 minutes will be subtracted from Sialkot time to find Riyadh time.
Calculation of Minutes
Quantity | Value; Sialkot time | = 12:00 pm; Difference of time between Sialkot and Riyadh | = -1 hour 56 minutes; Riyadh Time | = 10:04 am

4.9 Factors Affecting Agriculture Yield
There are 4 main factors that affect agriculture yield:
a) Soil Fertility
There are many nutrients which are essential for proper crop development. Soil is a major source of these nutrients to plants and therefore soil fertility has a profound impact on crop production.
b) Availability of water
The availability of water has a direct impact on agriculture yield. Little precipitation can reduce crop yield, while excessive precipitation can also cause crop production to decrease.
c) Climate
Climate is also important factor that influence crop production. Climatic conditions include humidity, temperature, wind etc.
d) Disease or Pests
Pests and diseases greatly influence crop yield as well. Certain pests also damage plant roots besides having a direct damage on crops.

Climate change due to enhanced greenhouse effect, arising as a result of activities of man is considered as a prime global environmental threat to humanity.
5.3 Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming

The natural warming of the surface of the earth and lower atmosphere due to the presence of greenhouse gases in the atmosphere, is called the Greenhouse Effect. This process occurs when greenhouse gases trap energy from the sun that reflect back into the atmosphere and stop some heat from going back into space. Water vapors, carbon dioxide and methane are the major greenhouse gases.
5.3 Greenhouse Effect and Global Warming
These gases are good absorbers of earth's radiation.
5.4 Impacts of Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming

The greenhouse effect is crucial because it makes life possible on earth. Without this greenhouse effect, the earth would be too cold to live on for most of the living creatures. But, however, excess of greenhouse gases are dangerous because they lead to global warming.
5.4 Impacts of Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming

The greenhouse gases are being produced by almost all human activities, such as agriculture, cutting of trees, household usages of refrigerators and air-conditioners, business activities like burning of fossil fuels in industries and vehicles. As more fossil fuels are burned, greenhouse gases enter the atmosphere and trap more heat.
5.4 Impacts of Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming

Consequently greenhouses gases, especially carbon dioxide levels rise in atmosphere and as a result, temperature of the earth as a whole increases. This increase in average temperature of the earth is called global warming.
5.4 Impacts of Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming

Most climate scientists think that increase in atmospheric carbon dioxide (mainly due to human activities) is the most important cause of global warming. Beside human activities, this increase in carbon dioxide can also be correlated with industrial revolution.

5.4 Impacts of Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming

Between 1906 and 2005, average temperature of the earth increased by 0.74°C. • 8 of the 10 warmest years on record occurred, since the year 2000. • Warm temperatures increase the amount of water vapour in the atmosphere. Water vapor is more powerful absorber of earth's radiation than carbon dioxide. • In polar areas and in rest of the world, ice and glaciers are melting fast due to global warming.
5.4 Impacts of Greenhouse Gases and Global Warming

The melting of ice increases the sea level. Sea ice reflects more incoming solar radiation than water. Therefore, conversion of ice into water will increase the temperature. • Average summer ice in the Arctic region has been decreasing at a rate of about 7.4% per decade, since the year 1978.
5.5 Importance of the Ozone Layer

Between 1900 and 2005, average precipitation increased in parts of North and South America, Northern Europe and Central and Northern Asia; while average precipitation decreased in Southern Africa, South Asia and the Mediterranean. Occurrences of floods are more likely in wetter areas and similarly occurrence of droughts are more likely in drier places.
5.5 Importance of the Ozone Layer

Ozone gas is naturally present in the atmosphere. Ozone concentration, which is often referred as ozone layer, is mainly found in the stratosphere. The presence of ozone layer is essential because it protects the earth from harmful ultraviolet radiations from the sun. Ultraviolet radiation can cause the risk of skin cancer, headaches, eye diseases and other health problems in humans.
5.5 Importance of the Ozone Layer
It can also damage the plant life and aquatic ecosystems. In short, life would be very difficult without the ozone layer.
5.6 Main Causes of Climate Change

Ozone layer has been destroyed by man-made chemicals especially Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs). CFCs are mainly used in refrigerators and air conditioners. Thus, human activities contribute to the thinning of ozone layer which is often called as ozone depletion. Severe depletion of ozone layer occured over Antarctica. This is called the 'ozone hole'.

Earth's crust is made of rocks and rocks are made of minerals. Minerals are substances that are formed naturally in the earth by geological processes such as volcanic action, heat or pressure. They are usually solid, inorganic and have a crystal structure. A mineral can be made of single element or more usually as compound. There are over 4,000 types of known minerals.

describe the collapse of Roman Empire (Western) in 476 CE and its major impacts. • discuss the salient features of Medieval Europe with a special focus on Western Europe. • explain how feudalism affected the socio-economic and political dynamics of Medieval Western Europe. • trace the spread of Christianity in Western Europe and describe its impacts on Europe.

• describe why Middle Ages is regarded sometimes as the Dark Ages for Western Europe. • introduce Byzantine Roman Empire (also called as Eastern Roman Empire) and its timeline. • explain the factors leading to the fall of Constantinople in 1453 and its impacts.
Middle Ages in Europe (500 AD to 1500 AD)

The gradual decline of the Roman Empire ushered in the Middle Ages which is also called Medieval period in European history. The Middle ages spanned from about 500 AD to 1500 AD. After the fall of Greek civilization, Roman Empire became the undisputed superpower of the Mediterranean by virtue of its strong military, technological advancement and widespread infrastructure.
Middle Ages in Europe (500 AD to 1500 AD)
The Roman Empire has left an indelible mark on the world.
Middle Ages in Europe (500 AD to 1500 AD)

Some historians argue that the Roman Empire never fully ended because the Eastern half of the Roman Empire sustained in the form of the Byzantine Empire. In this unit you will learn about the fall of the powerful Roman Empire, continuity of Byzantium Empire and the rise of European feudalism and Mongols.
Marcus Aurelius

Marcus Aurelius reigned from 161 CE to 180 CE and is best known as the last capable ruler of the Roman Empire. He always respected the Law. Despite numerous internal and external challenges, he managed to survive and preserved the Roman Empire.
The Decline of the Roman Empire

After the death of the emperor Marcus Aurelius in 180 AD, disorder shook the Roman Empire. Resultantly, the empire dissolved into many minor kingdoms in Western Europe. In the fifth century, Germanic invaders overran the western half of the Roman Empire. Repeated invasions and continuous warfare caused many changes in the economic conditions, governance and the culture of Romans.
The Decline of the Roman Empire
Here are some of the most significant causes that may help you understand how the Roman Empire declined and eventually fell apart.
The Decline of the Roman Empire

i. After the era of some capable rulers, for a couple of centuries, the Roman Empire was ruled by inefficient rulers. Especially after the death of Marcus Aurelius, his successors could not rule such a vast empire effectively. • ii. Barbarians infringed and settled themselves on the outskirts of the Roman Empire. With the passage of time, their power and influence increased.
The Decline of the Roman Empire
At last the Roman Empire crumbled to them in 476 AD.
Effects of the Fall of Roman Empire

iii. The Roman Empire was vast in size. In 285 CE, Emperor Diocletian decided to divide it into two parts: the Eastern Roman Empire and the Western Roman Empire. In contrast to the Eastern Roman Empire, the government in the West was corrupt causing poverty and unemployment throughout the empire. • iv. Famines and plagues hit the Roman Empire. The problem was worsened by the high taxes.
Effects of the Fall of Roman Empire
It resulted in starvation, deaths and violence.
Facts to Know

Inform the students that the decline and fall of the Roman Empire is divided into two parts: the first half covers approximately 300 years until the end of the empire in the West and the second half constricts nearly 1,000 years.
Facts to Know

Germanic Tribes: The Germanic people were nomadic tribes who lived in northern Europe. They had a powerful military. The Romans referred to them collectively as Germans because most of them spoke a language based on common Germanic, even though they represented a wide variety of nationalities and cultures.
Facts to Know

Barbarian: Barbarian was the term used by the Romans to describe people who lived outside of the empire. Goaths, Visigoths, Vandals, Huns, and other tribes resided in the empire. These Barbarian tribes arrived in Rome from Central Asia and other European region settled themselves in the empire.
Effects of the Fall of Roman Empire

Many historians see the fall of the Western Roman Empire as the end of the ancient world and the beginning of the Middle Ages. When the infrastructure was destroyed due to invasions, the quality of governance and people's lives declined as well. What followed was the Dark Ages which impacted the whole of the Western Europe greatly. Some of the important impacts are as under:
Feudalism

With the collapse of Romans rule in 476 AD, the centralized structure of the empire vanished. As a result, a number of tribal cheifdoms emerged. The collapse of centralized authority led to the rise of feudal states in Europe. • The barbarian invasions destroyed entire socio-economic infrastructure.
Feudalism

However, the Church as an entity survived and provided some order and security during this time of political instability. Ultimately, the Pope rose to become the most powerful religious and political figure in Western Europe.
Feudalism

Although, Western Roman Empire collapsed and fragmented into hundreds of chiefdoms and kingdoms, the Eastern Roman Empire grew into the Byzantium Empire with Orthodox Christianity as the official religion.
Feudalism

Trade was disrupted because merchants were attacked from both land and sea routes. Their businesses were doomed. The breakdown of trade devastated Europe's economic hubs. Money was increasingly scarce.
Feudalism

Advancement in learning slowed down. Only priests, church officials, and a few others could read Greek works, literature and science and philosophy. Medieval age is generally known for the decline in literacy and learning. • Latin languages were no longer understood because Germanic-speaking people mixed with the Roman population. French, Spanish, and other Roman based languages emerged from Latin.
Feudalism

The continued disintegration of a once unified empire was reflected in the creation of numerous languages. The society was fragmented and disunited until the 700 AD, when Kings, lords and nobles established some order in the land through the system of feudalism.
Facts to Know
There are approximately 2.3 billion Christians worldwide with approximately 1.3 billion of them being Roman Catholics.
Feudalism

Feudalism is a political and economic system based on land ownership and personal loyalty. It was the need of the day to bring the politically fractured society back together. Almost everyone lived in a small town or village. Feudalism helped in the creation of order in Western Europe. Feudalism arose in Western Europe after the fall of the Roman Empire.
Feudalism
The rise of European feudalism was the direct outcome of political disorder and continued warfare.
Note for Teachers
Ask students to watch a documentary on fall of Roman Empire and share their findings in the class.
Effects of Feudalism on Medieval Europe

The feudal system was founded on the principle of rights and obligations in order to govern the kingdom effectively. Social classes were well defined. The system looked like a pyramid in which the king, church, lords, and peasants were associated to each other according to their role, power and prestige in the society. The King and the Pope both enjoyed supreme positions.
Effects of Feudalism on Medieval Europe

The most powerful vassals, wealthy landowners or nobles and bishops came next. Knights were mounted horsemen who promised to defend the lands of their masters in exchange for fiefs. Landless peasants worked in the fields. Although the Roman Church was one of the main unifying features in Medieval times, However due to the lack of knowledge about the laws of nature, many people were led to irrational beliefs.
European Feudalism had three main characteristics:
Political: The King commanded absolute power based on God's will. The Catholic Church held considerable power in government affairs.
European Feudalism had three main characteristics:
Economic: People had specific jobs that they had to do for their entire lives.
European Feudalism had three main characteristics:
Social: The feudal pyramid was a social structure of a hierarchical nature. Some individuals were more important than others.
Manors: The Economic Side of Feudalism

During the Middle Ages, the manor system was the primary economic structure. The manor was the name given to the lord's estate. Under the manor system, a lord and his serfs had a set of rights and responsibilities. The landlord provided the serfs with houses, farmland, and protection from bandits. Serfs helped to maintain the estate by administering the lands, caring for his animals and other jobs.
Manors: The Economic Side of Feudalism

They owed the lord specific duties, including working at least a couple of days and giving their lords a portion of their grain. Peasants paid heavy price for the privilege of living on the lord's land.

The Role of Warrior in Feudal Society

By the 11th century, Western Europe had become a battleground of feuding nobility seeking for dominance. Feudal lords raised private armies of knights or Cavalry to defend their lands. The code of chivalry, a complicated set of beliefs, required a knight to battle bravely in defence of his master. The weak and poor were likewise safeguarded by the gallant knight.
Significance of Feudalism
Feudalism functioned as a hierarchical system. It greatly helped Western Europe for the following reasons:
Significance of Feudalism

Feudalism protected the society of Western Europe from the violence and warfare that erupted after the fall of Rome, as well as from powerful invaders. • Feudalism facilitated the restoration of trade. Roads and bridges were repaired. The knights maintained the rule of law and made it safe to travel on roads. • Feudalism prohibited a single person organization from gaining power.
Significance of Feudalism
The power was distributed among many individuals and groups. This was probably the precursor to European concepts of limited power for the government, constitutions, and civil rights.
Limitations of Feudalism
European feudalism did not always work well in practice because:
Limitations of Feudalism

Feudalism provided local unity and security but was unable to unite larger regions or countries in Europe. • In the absence of a strong central government, it was easy to subjugate the poor through force and violence in feudal system. • Feudalism did not treat people equally or allow them to progress in their own society.
Limitations of Feudalism
A person born a serf or lord was expected to remain a serf or lord for the rest of his or her life.

The history of the Catholic Church begins with the teachings of Jesus Christ. The Christian Church in Roman cities developed and organized into a hierarchy. The priests and clergy obeyed the Church.

Role of the Roman Catholic Church in the Life of Ordinary People

During the Middle Ages, the Roman Catholic Church grew in wealth and influence. According to the doctrine of Roman Catholic Church, the Pope held absolute and unlimited power over the entire Church. At the same time, the Roman Catholic Church provided stability and leadership on which people could rely. For instance, the King Charlemagne of France was the most powerful monarch of the Holy Roman Empire.
Role of the Roman Catholic Church in the Life of Ordinary People
In 800 AD, he was crowned as Frankish emperor by Pope Leo III. In the following years, the Pope's dominance compelled numerous monarchs to work with the Church.
Role of the Roman Catholic Church in the Life of Ordinary People

The Church exerted significant influence and control over ordinary people. Holidays were observed to commemorate saints or religious events. Church leaders were in charge of schools, hospitals and tax collection. Priests registered births, married people, and officiated at funerals.
The Byzantine Empire (330 AD to 1453 AD)

The Byzantine Empire also called the Eastern Roman Empire, existed from 330 AD to 1453 AD. The Byzantine Empire was the continuation of the Roman Empire in its eastern provinces during the Middle Ages.
Note for Teachers
Ask the students to study the hierarchy carefully and discuss why was the hierarchy, shown in the pyramid, important in the Roman Catholic society?
Justinian Code

Eastern Europe and Russia were introduced to Greco-Roman culture, Greek language, and Eastern Orthodox Christianity by the Byzantine civilization. The Hagia Sophia was the Orthodox Patriarch's seat in Constantinople, which is now Istanbul.
Justinian Code

Justinian Code is one of the most notable achievements of Byzantine Empire. During the reign of Emperor Justinian I (527 AD - 565 AD) the ancient Roman laws were collected and organised to form the Justinian Code. The Justinian Code brought uniformity to the majority of the laws that comprise the modern world's justice system.
Economy and Trade

The Byzantine Empire had a strong agricultural and trade-based economy. Constantinople was regarded as the trade centre because it controlled the major trade routes connecting Europe and Asia. Direct commercial contacts were maintained in Constantinople with merchants from Central Asia, Russia, Scandinavia, Northern Europe, and the Black Sea and Mediterranean Sea.
Economy and Trade
Even after the conquest of Arab lands, the Empire traded with Persia, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt, except when at war with them.

The Decline of the Byzantine Empire

According to historians, no single event brought the Byzantine Empire to an end. Natural disasters and powerful enemies such as the Arabs, Seljuk Turks, and Ottoman Turks all contributed to the empire's demise. Most importantly, the Byzantine Empire's incessant civil wars destroyed a highly efficient military system, a sizable population, trade network, and economy.
The Decline of the Byzantine Empire
While the empire was declining, civil wars hastened its demise. With the fall of Constantinople, the Russian Empire became the centre of Eastern European society and Orthodox Christianity.
Facts to Know: Fall of Constantinople 1453

Fall of Constantinople in 1453 is considered to be the end of Byzantine Empire. This was the year when Ottoman Sultan Mehmet Fatih conquered the ancient city of constantinople. The city was renamed as Islambul which became Istanbul in the later years. You may get more information about this city through different sources.
The Dark Ages and Impacts on Europe

The term "Dark Ages" 500 AD-1000 AD is frequently used interchangeably with "Middle Ages." It refers to the time between the fall of the Roman Empire and the beginning of the Renaissance. The Dark Ages were also characterized by frequent warfare between Barbarians and Mongols.
Significant Impacts of Dark Ages on Europe
Despite the fact that there was little scientific and cultural progress during this time period, some significant impacts were well known such as:
Significant Impacts of Dark Ages on Europe

i. Catholic Christianity flourished in Western Europe during this time period. • ii. The Roman Empire gradually disintegrated into many smaller political entities or empires. Feudalism remained the dominant political system in Western Europe. • iii. The most wealthy and powerful members of society created cathedrals, churches, sculpture, painting, textiles, manuscripts, jewellery, and ritual items. • iv.
Significant Impacts of Dark Ages on Europe
The Byzantine Empire remained a powerful political entity in the East.
The Rise of Mongol Empire

As Europe lived through the Middle Ages, the world witnessed the rise of the Mongols in Asia. Indeed, the Mongol conquests between the early-13th and mid-14th centuries dominated world history. The Mongols were a nomadic warring people from Central Asia. The Mongol era is best known for its overwhelming military power. Genghis Khan had conquered much of Central Asia by 1127 AD.
The Rise of Mongol Empire

As they moved south and took control of Persia, the Genghis Khan's successors made various conquests. In 1258, his grandson Halako Khan attacked Baghdad and destroyed the Abbassid Caliphate; you can read more about this in the Islamic history chapters.
The Rise of Mongol Empire

The Mongols divided the regions into four groups known as khanates in 1260. This facilitated them to efficiently govern the vast territory of the empire. Until 1294, the Mongols ruled the world's largest unified empire.
Impacts of Mongols Invasions on Europe

After establishing their rule, the Mongols allowed the people to retain their local institutions and cultures. The Catholic Christian church of Western Europe maintained control of their territory. The Mongol network greatly facilitated travel and communication between Asia and Europe.
Impacts of Mongols Invasions on Europe

During the Mongol era, travellers such as Marco Polo brought back information about China and provided access to Chinese technologies such as coal for energy, money, printing and explosive powder, astronomy, medicine, and mathematics. The tax system was established by the Mongols. Banking and insurance practices spread from Eurasia to Europe, resulting in economic stability in these parts of the world.
Impacts of Mongols Invasions on Europe

However, the faster inter-regional contact during the Mongol period created a serious problem. During this time, the Black Death or Plague began in China and quickly spread to the Middle East and Europe. The plague killed one-quarter to one-third of the population of Western Europe and the Middle East.
Do You Know?

In the late 13th century, Marco Polo, a young Venetian explorer, embarked on a grand adventure to China. He met and served in the army of the Great Khan, Kublai Khan. During his years under Kublai's patronage, Marco Polo introduced the Great Khan to European civilization, and the Great Khan, in turn, introduced Marco Polo to Chinese civilization.
Decline of the Mongol Empire

According to historical records, Mongol or Khan dynasty ended in 1368. The Mongol empire ceased to expand and began to decline after the death of Kublai Khan. The succession issue, internal disputes, lack of leadership, and widespread corruption contributed to the downfall of Mongol Empire. In the end, the Khanates were defeated by external enemies and disintegrated.
Decline of the Mongol Empire
Nonetheless, the Mongol Empire, particularly in terms of technology exchange, has continued to have an impact on the world.

Facts to Remember

Mumluk dynasty of Egypt defeated Mongols in the battle of Ain Jalut in 1260. Mongols could not advance further in the Muslim world. Mumluks were militarily very powerful to the extent that they defeated numerous crusaders.

Establishment of Umayyad Dynasty (661 to 750)

The name of this dynasty comes from its founder Hazrat Mu'awiya ibn Abu Sufyan (RA) who was from the Banu Umayya branch of the Quraysh tribe. Umayya was the great grandfather of Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA) who was a famous commander of pre-Islamic Arabia who was originally from Makkah.
Establishment of Umayyad Dynasty (661 to 750)

After the departure of Rasulullah (PBUH), the golden period of Pious Caliphate continued till 661 AD. This was the year of martyrdom of the fourth pious caliph Hazrat Ali (RA) when people gave their pledges to Hazrat Hassan ibn Ali (RA). During the caliphate of Hazrat Ali (RA), Governor of Syria was Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA) who was a very strong leader. Some people wanted him to be the caliph.
Establishment of Umayyad Dynasty (661 to 750)

Keeping in view the importance of unity of the Muslim community, Hazrat Hassan (RA) decided to give his pledge to Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA). It was indeed a great sacrifice of Hazrat Hassan (RA) for unity of Muslim Umma. This marked the start of the rule of the Umayyad Dynasty which lasted from 661 to 750 AD. Syria remained the Umayyads' main power base and Damascus became the new capital of the caliphate.
Do You Know?
The year in which Hazrat Hassan (RA) gave his pledge to Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA) and established unity of the Muslims, is called "Am al-Jama'" (The year of Unification).

Umayyads and Expansion of the Muslim State

During the Umayyad Caliphate, Muslim State expanded significantly. Till that time, the Muslim armies were available in Syria, Iraq and Egypt. Armies in Syria fought in the lands of Anatolia and Armenia, which at that time, were under the control of the Byzantine Empire. The armies in Iraq fought and conquered Khurasan, Sindh and the armies in Egypt fought in North Africa.
Umayyads and Expansion of the Muslim State
At its greatest extent, the Umayyad Caliphate covered around 5.80 million square miles and its population was 62 million people (almost 30% of the world's population of that time).
Note for Teachers

Inform the students that the most prominent rulers of Ummayad Caliphate were Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA), Hazrat Umer Bin Abdul Aziz, and Waleed Bin Abdul Malik. Encourage the students to learn more about these rulers.
Expeditions in Anatolia

One of the most important accomplishments of Hazrat Muawiya (RA) was the building of a strong navy to weaken the strength of the Byzantine Empire in the eastern Mediterranean. A navy was built which captured Rhodes and other islands in the eastern Mediterranean in 671 AD.
Expeditions in Anatolia

In 674 AD, Constantinople, the capital of the Byzantine Empire, was besieged. The Muslim armies continued this besiege from 674 to 678 AD but were later forced back to eastern Anatolia. One of the most famous martyrs of this war was Hazrat Abu Ayyub Al Ansari (RA) who was still out in the path of Allah at the age of 80.
Expeditions in Anatolia

Later, during the period of Caliph Abdul Malik Bin Marwan, Armenia was also conquered which was under Byzantine rule. During the time of Suleman Bin Abdul Malik, Constantinople was sieged both from the sea and the land. However, this attempt of conquering the city also remained unsuccessful.
Eastern Front

On eastern front, armies were sent to Khurasan and Sindh by Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA). Later, under Sultan Abdul Malik (685–705 AD), the Muslim armies invaded Makran and Sindh in the Subcontinent. In Central Asia they conquered Bukhara, Samarkand, Khwarazm, Fergana, and Tashkant.
Eastern Front
Many of these conquests came in the time of great Muslim general Qutayba Bin Muslim who was also governor of Khurasan during the reign of Walid Bin Abdul Malik (705 AD to 715 AD).
Eastern Front
Another important conquest during the time of Caliph Walid was of Sindh. Muhammad Bin Qasim conquered Sindh in 711-712 AD. This marked the beginning of Muslim presence in the Subcontinent.
Note for Teachers

Inform the students that Anatolia is the region that encompasses the central uplands of modern Turkey, from the coastal plain of the Aegean Sea east to the mountains on the Armenian border and from the narrow coast of the Black Sea south to the Taurus Mountains and Mediterranean coast.
Muhammad Bin Qasim

Muhammad Bin Qasim was born in 695 AD. He was a close relative of Hajjaj Bin Yousaf, the governor of Iraq. He belonged to Taif region of Arabia. These were his skills that helped Muhammad Bin Qasim in being appointed as the governor of Persia while he was still in his teens.
Muhammad Bin Qasim

After the advent of Islam, the Arab traders brought Islam in the south Asia and Southeast Asia. The relations between the Arabs and the Indian Subcontinent were smooth. However, the sea borne trade of the Arabs in the Indian Ocean was threatened when Raja Dahir allied with the ruler of Makran and Persia against the Muslims.
Muhammad Bin Qasim
It was the first time when Arabs, during Umayyad dynasty, made serious attempts to conquer Sindh.
Reasons for the Invasion of Sindh by Arabs
In the oldest chronicles of Arabs' conquest of Sindh, two main reasons are highlighted for the invasion of Sindh:
Reasons for the Invasion of Sindh by Arabs

i. The sea pirates raided off the coast of Debal and looted all the valuables and plundered several ships travelling to Arabia. These pirates also abducted some innocent women and children. Upon hearing this, Hajjaj bin Yusuf, the governor of Iraq, wrote a letter to Raja Dahir and demanded the recovery of the goods and Muslim captives. • ii.
Reasons for the Invasion of Sindh by Arabs
Hajjaj bin Yusuf also demanded the return of the exiled Arab offenders, who after murdering the governor of Makran, took refuge in Sindh.
Reasons for the Invasion of Sindh by Arabs

Since no compromise could be reached between Raja Dahir and Hajjaj Bin Yusuf tension continued to increase. At that point, the Governor Hajjaj Bin Yusuf decided to launch a military expedition under the command of Muhammad Bin Qasim with a powerful army to fight Raja Dahir of Sindh.
Conquest of Sindh

Muhammad Bin Qasim travelled all the way to Makran, where he was joined by many local Jats and Meds. Very importantly, Buddhists welcomed Muhammad Bin Qasim because they suffered great persecution under Raja Dahir's rule.
Conquest of Sindh

Muhammad Bin Qasim first marched to Debal which was a strongly fortified city. The Arab forces fought bravely. With the help of Catapults, Arab forces pulled down the red flag waving over a large temple as a symbol of political power and unity. This shocked and (continues on the next page)
Governance in Sindh Under the Arabs
... demoralized Raja Dahir's army and soon the city fell into Arabs' hands.
Governance in Sindh Under the Arabs

Muhammad Bin Qasim marched inland through the banks of Indus River. Other cities also surrendered or were captured. In the great battle of Aror, Raja Dahir was also killed. Muhammad bin Qasim's forces defeated the remaining enemies within months, and all of Sindh fell under Arab rule and remained so for the next few centuries.
Governance in Sindh Under the Arabs
Historians note that Arab rule over Sindh was very different from Raja Dahir's rule. The most important changes were:
Governance in Sindh Under the Arabs

1. Local people were treated kindly as Muhammad Bin Qasim followed a peace-making policy for all the natives of Sindh. This allowed everyone to practice their religion openly without any danger of persecution. • 2. He imposed taxes on locals and in return they were provided the guarantee of the security of their life and property. • 3.
Governance in Sindh Under the Arabs

The religious shrines such as temples were also protected from any attack or damage. • 4. Hindus were allowed to rule their villages and settle their disputes according to their own laws. As a strategy Muhammad Bin Qasim also incorporated the local elites and ex officials of Dahir's administration. This made his rule stronger and effective. • 5. Non-Muslim natives were exempted from military service.
Governance in Sindh Under the Arabs

The trade between Southeast Asia and the Subcontinent increased gradually. Unfortunately, as the years went by, the leadership in Arabia grew weaker. This allowed many local governors of Sindh to break free from the Arab rule and become independent.
Muhammad bin Qasim and the Spread of Islam in the Subcontinent

The conquest of Sindh paved the way for spread of Islam in the Subcontinent. It is important to note that many of the local people who embraced Islam were from lower castes, who were attracted to the egalitarian nature of Islam. Later, several Masajid and Madaris were built in cities and towns. Resultantly, in a short period, Sindh became a center of Islamic learning.
Conquests in Africa

Islam became an evolving religion of the Subcontinent. Many influential people accepted Islam which influenced the common people. The spread of Islam was further helped by the sufi saints who spread the message of love, peace, and tolerance through their teachings. It was because of their efforts that Islam became the second biggest religion of the Subcontinent in few centuries.
Conquests in Africa

Although Muhammad Bin Qasim only conquered the northwestern part of the Subcontinent, tolerant behaviour of the Muslim rulers impressed many to embrace Islam in that region. This provided a solid base for further Muslim expansion into India.
Conquests in Africa

Earlier started conquests in Africa continued during Umayyad caliphate. A great Muslim commander Uqba Bin Nafay conquered many parts of Africa that included present-day Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Morocco up to the Atlantic shores.

Discuss with class the Islamic principles of peaceful co-existence with diverse communities after the war. • Inform the students that this historic Muhammad Bin Qasim Masjid is just one of the many which needs our attention. Discuss with students about the ways to draw the attention of the government for the revival and restoration of this monument.
Conquests in Spain

Later during the reign of Walid Bin Abdul Malik, Musa Bin Nuseyr and Tariq Bin Ziyad achieved great victories in Africa and Spain. Tariq Bin Ziyad conquered Spain in 711 when he defeated King Roderick.
Conquests in Spain

In 750 AD, Ummayad rule in Damascus ceased to exist and was replaced by the Abbasids. However, the rule of Ummayad was renewed in 756 in Spain which continued till 1492. During this period Spain became a centre of education, art and architecture. This rule is also known for religious tolerance.
Facts to Know

Ummayad's rule in Spain is considered to be a golden period of this region. The prominent rulers of this age were Abdul Rahman-I and Abdul Rahman-III. Use different sources to find about the art, architecture, literature, science and technology of that era which was introduced by the Mulims in Spain.
Conquests in Spain

During the time of Caliph Umar Bin Abdul Aziz, many Berbers in North Africa embraced Islam because of his kind behaviour towards the minorities. By the end of Umayyad period, the Muslim world extended from the Atlantic Ocean to Spain in the west and to Central Asia and the Subcontinent in the east.
Development of Islamic Art and Culture

The Umayyad period is considered to be a critical period in the development of Islamic art and culture. The Umayyads gave great importance to education and opened many houses of scholars, bookstores and schools.
Architecture

Art of that era was influenced by multiple sources. These include Coptic tradition of present-day Egypt and Syria, Sassanian metalwork and crafts from what is now Iraq, and Byzantine mosaics depicting animals and plants. Despite all this, Muslim architects produced original works based on their beliefs. The Umayyads are considered to be pioneers in Islamic Art.
Architecture
Tradition of adding minarets and mihrab to the Masajid began with the Umayyads.
Architecture

A beautiful example of such work is Dome of the Rock (Kubbat al-Sahra) in Jerusalem. It was one of the first Islamic buildings ever constructed. It was built between 685 and 692 by Abd al-Malik. The mosaics in the Dome of the Rock contain no human figures or animals. You can see its picture on the first page of this chapter.
Architecture

Another piece of early Islamic art that survived till today is Umayyad Mosque in Damascus. Its construction was started by Walid-I in 706 AD which was finished in 715 AD during the reign of Suleman bin Abdul Malik.
Do You Know?
Which famous poem was written by Allama Muhammad Iqbal while sitting in the Great Masjid of Cordoba? What was its message?
Language and Literature

Umayyads made great contribution in the fields of language and literature. The Holy Quran was originally written without punctuation (Aarab). In order to help non-Arabs understand Quran easily, method of punctuation was adopted by the Umayyads. Poetry also got great development during that time where many caliphs promoted it.
Language and Literature
Arabic language was specially promoted and during the caliphate of Abdul Malik, Arabic was declared as official language. This helped to promote Arabic as language of scholarship.
Sciences

A huge number of scientific works were translated into Arabic, mostly from Greek language, during the Umayyad period. Khalid Ibn Yazid brought some scholars from Alexandria to Damascus and established a great library there. Khalid himself translated works of Chemistry and medicine into Arabic. In Andalusia, the Muslims were at advanced level of religious disciplines as well as other scholarly subjects.
Sciences

Literacy was very high in Andalusia. According to various historical sources, there were four hundred thousand books in the library of Cordoba. Great Masjid of Cordoba, Madinat uz Zahra Masjid and Alhambra Palace are few of the well-known monuments of that period.
Administration and Economic System

Consolidation of the Muslim state was first task of Hazrat Mu'awiya (RA). Political and military affairs, tax collection, and religious administration were three main branches of the administration of government.
Administration
The empire was divided into several provinces where governors were appointed to run administration. Tax collection, religious affairs, law and order, and civil administration was under the governors.
Economy

During the reign of Umayyad caliphs, due to expansion of the borders, the trade size increased. Foreign trade expanded and agriculture advanced significantly. Monetary policies were renewed, and new methods of irrigation, fertilization, and crop rotation were adopted. Umayyads maintained the roads for trade and military movement.
Currency

Umayyad leaders continued using coin system of the Byzantine and Sassanid Empires. Coins had phrases from the Quran stamped on them. These were the first coins in history, minted by a Muslim government. Dinars were made of gold while dirhams were made of silver.
Hazrat Umar Bin Abdul Aziz

He remained caliph from 717 to 720 AD. His caliphate will be remembered as revival of the spirit of pious caliphate. His governance was a symbol of equality and public welfare. He appointed his governors based on their uprightness. He gave greater importance to Qazis (judges) thus kept the flag of justice always high.

Agriculture

Agriculture remained an important part of the state economy during the caliphate of the Umayyads. Famous governor Hajjaj Bin Yusuf embarked on digging up rivers and canals in Iraq, reclaiming agriculture land and building up towns in the reclaimed areas. Thousands of working cattle and agricultural labourers were brought from other areas to establish new communities on the new land.
Agriculture
In Egypt too, families were brought from other provinces to develop areas in Lower Egypt.
Trade

Expansion of the Islamic State opened many new markets all the way from China to Europe for the Muslims. The trade goods included food products, timber, metals, textiles, stones, sea food, and medicines. Trade routes connected Europe with the Islamic world mainly via Syria, Egypt, Tunisia and Sicily.
Tax System

Structure of finance and taxing remained almost the same as that during the pious caliphate. Caliph Umar Bin Abdul Aziz proposed a major revision of the rules and principles of taxation in order to achieve uniformity. The caliph Hisham followed the policies of Caliph Umar Bin Abdul Aziz and introduced the same tax reforms in Khurasan, Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Reasons Leading to the Downfall of the Umayyad Dynasty

The Umayyad caliphate collapsed in 750 AD after a rule of about 90 years. The last 30 years of the caliphate witnessed great opposition of the Abbasids. This was not the only cause of downfall of the Umayyads but there were many other factors too that caused their decline. Some of these factors are stated as under:
a) Lifestyle of Leaders

Some of the caliphs in this dynasty spent their lives in a lavish manner which repulsed people. The groups which were against the regime, got benefit from this situation and provoked people against this weakness of the Umayyads.
b) The Disgrace of the Nobles

With the arrival of the new caliph, the administrators and nobles of the previous regime were maltreated. Great generals Musa Bin Nusayr, Muhammad Bin Qasim and Qutayba Bin Muslim were maltreated by the new caliph Suleman Bin Abdul Malik. This and such other incidents destroyed the spirit of loyalty from the key figures.
c) Discrimination Against Mawalis (Non-Arab Muslims)

During the caliphate of the Umayyads, the Mawalis were treated as second class citizens. They were kept away from government positions. Heavy taxes on them caused great social unrest and resulted in helping the rebellions against the Umayyads.
d) Ignoring Scholarly Activities

One of the issues that bore negative consequences for Umayyads was their neglect of scholarly activities. The scholarly mawalis who were cornered by the Umayyads became brain of the opposition and joined rebellions.
e) Internal Conflicts

Another important cause of decline of Umayyad dynasty was their internal conflicts. These conflicts mostly arose for the succession and power. Many provinces revolted. These internal conflicts strengthened the rivals so much that within few years, whole dynasty collapsed.
Establishment of Abbasid Dynasty

The Abbasids came into power after the Umayyads. The Abbasids ruled Muslim Empire from 750 to 1258 AD. This dynasty took its name from the uncle of Rasulullah (PBUH) Hazrat Abbas (RA). His great-grandson, Muhammad ibn 'Ali, started the movement of return of power to the Hashimites, during the caliphate of Hazrat Umar bin Abdul Aziz who ruled from 717 to 720 AD.
Establishment of Abbasid Dynasty
This campaign got support from mawalis, the non-Arab Muslims, who were cornered by the Umayyads.
Establishment of Abbasid Dynasty

Earlier in this unit, you have studied about the causes of the downfall of Umayyad dynasty. These causes paved the way for Abbasid dynasty. Their first success was in Khurasan and then in Kufa in 749 AD where Abul Abbas became the first caliph of Abbasid dynasty. Later, Abbasid army entered Syria and defeated Umayyad army under their last ruler Marwan II in 750 AD.
Establishment of Abbasid Dynasty
This year is the start of Abbasid dynasty that continued for next many centuries.
Do You Know?
The Islamic Golden Age was a period of cultural, economic and scientific flourishing in the history of Islam, traditionally dating from the 8th century to the 13th century.
