Foundation of the New Capital

After the death of the founder of Abbasid dynasty, Abu Al Abbas in 754 AD, the second caliph of this dynasty was Abu Jafar al-Mansur. He organized administration to strengthen Abbasid's rule. After eliminating internal threats, Al Mansur founded a new city on the banks of the Tigris river. This was Baghdad that remained centre of learning for many years to come as the capital of the Islamic Empire.
Abbasids and the non-Arabs

The main feature of Abbasid administration was giving important positions to mawalis or the non-Arabs. After declaring Baghdad as their capital, the Abbasid caliphs established the office of the vizier as the most powerful authority after caliph. Mawali viziers were appointed to this position. Khalid Barmaki of the Persian origin was appointed as head of both the Diwan al Kharaj and Diwan al Jund.
Abbasids and the non-Arabs
(You have studied about these administrative offices in the previous section). Yahya Barmaki of the same family remained governor of Azerbaijan and then Vizier of Caliph Harun al Rashid.
Abbasids and the non-Arabs

Turks were also awarded important positions during Abbasid caliphate. They started getting dominance during the reign of Mamun al Rashid. Later, his brother Mu'tasim became caliph with Turkish support. He shifted capital from Baghdad to Samarra in 836 AD thus began the Period of Samarra which lasted till 892 AD.
Abbasid Achievements in the Field of Science

The greatest contribution of Abbasid to Islamic civilization was in the fields of science. Abbasid caliphs gave great importance to scientists. Baghdad, the capital of the Abbasid Empire, became centre of intellectual and scientific learning. A house of wisdom with the name Bayt al-Hikmah was established by the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid and further flourished by Mamun al Rashid.
Abbasid Achievements in the Field of Science

This was a great evidence of support of Abbasids for science. Within few decades Baghdad became a centre of learning. Many educational institutions, hospitals, masjids, and libraries made Baghdad an attraction for students from different parts of the world.
Note for Teachers

Inform the students that the most prominent rulers of Abbasid Caliphate were Abu Jaffar Mansoor, Haroon ur Rasheed, Mamoon ur Rasheed and Mu'tasim Billah. Encourage the students to learn more about these rulers.
Translation Movement

After the dawn of the Abbasid rule, translations from Greek, Syriac, Persian and Sanskrit opened the doors of knowledge for the Muslim world. Though this translation movement had been started during Umayyad period, it flourished during Abbasids time. During the caliphate of Mamun al Rashid, the House of Wisdom was turned into an institute of translation.
Translation Movement
Texts on mathematics, astronomy, astrology and medicine were translated over the years. This translation movement played an important role in the development of Arab scientific knowledge.
Muslim Scientists

The tenth and eleventh centuries AD witnessed many Muslim scholars who contributed to the world of knowledge. Some of the best-known intellectuals of that time were Al-Razi, Ibn Sina, Al-Khwarizmi, Al-Beruni and Jabir Bin Hayyan. There were many other scientists too who played important role in spreading light of knowledge to the world.
Muslim Scientists

Abu Bakr Muhammad al-Razi (854–935 AD) was a physician, philosopher and chemist. Most of his works in medical field were translated into Latin and circulated widely in Europe. He wrote 237 books but most of them are extinct today. Sirr Al-asrar (Secret of Secrets) is Razi's most famous book which has gained a lot of recognition.
Muslim Scientists

Ibn Sina (980–1037 AD) studied Qur'anic sciences and Islamic jurisprudence before engaging with geometry, logic, other aspects of philosophy and medicine. Two of his most famous works which survived are the Book of Healing [of the Soul], a philosophical compendium, and the Canon of Medicine, a comprehensive medical work.
Muslim Scientists

Al-Khwarizmi (750-825 AD), a mathematician and astronomer, explained the use of zero and advanced the decimal system. He introduced important mathematical terms like "algebra" and "algorithm". Al-Khwarizmi is also known as father of Algebra.
Muslim Scientists

Abu Reyhan Muhammad Ibne Ahmed al-Beruni (973-1052) is considered as one of great Muslim scientists till date. He wrote around 150 books, most of which were on Mathematics and astronomy. His other works are on Physics, anthropology, pharmacology, minerology and history. His compendium of India; "Kitab al-Hind; Kitab al-Bīrūnī fī Taḥqīq mā li-al-Hind" provides an insight of Indian philosophy and religion.
Promotion of Art and Architecture

Jabir bin Hayyan (721-815 AD) is called father of Chemistry. He was universally recognized both in Muslims as well as in the Western world. He is considered to be innovator of many crafts like preserving leather, dyeing, waterproofing cloth, mining and oil purification. Jabir wrote more than 300 books on Chemistry and many of them were translated into Latin.
Promotion of Art and Architecture
Science thrived for two centuries in the Abbasid caliphate. However, this enthusiasm could not be continued in later Abbasid period.
Promotion of Art and Architecture

During the Golden Period of the Muslims, Islamic art and architecture grew with the discovery of new methods and technologies. With conquest on new lands and increasing influence of other civilizations, the Muslims had new sources of inspiration. However, the Muslim artisans improved their own aesthetics and created a whole new art style that is unique to the Islamic world.
Promotion of Art and Architecture

In fact, during the Abbasid period, Muslim styles of art, architecture and literature developed significantly. Great artists and architects made contributions under the patronage of caliph. Not only original Arab literature thrived but Greek, Persian and Sanskrit texts were translated into Arabic. Magnificent masjids were built by skilful architects during this period.
Promotion of Art and Architecture
Craftsmen showed their skill at making brilliant pots, glassware, fabrics, leather, and objects made of silver, copper and bronze.
Poetry

Most of the Arab world's most famous literary figures have been poets. Just like in the courts of Damascus, in Baghdad too, poets were held in the highest of regard. Ibn Nuwas and Al-Mutanabbi were two of the most famous Arab court poets during Abbasid caliphate. The Revival of Religious Sciences by Ghazali is yet another marvel and one of the most quoted texts.
Poetry
In Persian language, Omar Khayyam wrote his famous Rubayyiat which is very famous in the west too. The great poet Firdousi wrote his poetry during tenth and eleventh century.

Architecture

One of the major architectural activities of the Abbasid caliphs was building large new cities. The most important of these cities was Baghdad. About 2.7 kilometres, Baghdad was surrounded by mud-brick walls. Another city was al-Rafiqa that was constructed by al-Mansur. It was protected by a wall, nearly 5 kilometres.
Architecture

City of Samaraa was located around 125 kilometres North of Baghdad. This city served as capital of the Abbasids for a brief period during ninth century AD. The city was constructed by Mu'tasim, the son of Haroon-ur-Rashid.
Architecture

In addition to cities, some grand Masjids were also built during that period. Caliph al-Moutawakel build a huge Masjid in Samaraa with total area of 41 acres. For many centuries it was the largest masjid in the world.
Architecture
Another marvel of Abbasid architecture is Ibn Talun Masjid in Cairo. It was built by Ibn Talun who was governor of Egypt and Syria in 869 AD.
Architecture
Abbasid Palace of Ukhaider is located roughly 50 km south of Karbala, Iraq. It is a large, rectangular fortress erected in 775 AD with a unique defensive style.
Decline of Abbasid Caliphate

The periods of Caliphs Mansur, Mehdi, Harun Rashid, Ma'mun Rashid, and Mu'tasim is considered as "golden era" of the Abbasids. Foundations of Islamic civilizations were laid mostly during this period. The period of decline that started in 9th century continued until collapse of Abbasids in 1258 AD. There were many factors behind this decline that include both internal as well as external factors.
Decline of Abbasid Caliphate
Some of the important factors are as under:
Decline of Abbasid Caliphate

1. Differences among various groups caused continuous unrest. Ethnic, political and regional disputes weakened the state. As the state expanded significantly, Arabs, Persians, Syrians, Berber, Christians, Jewish and Turks had open differences with each other that caused continuous conspiracies against the rulers. • 2. Luxurious lifestyle of the rulers destroyed their military virtues.
Decline of Abbasid Caliphate

Reign of early Abbasids is considered as golden period of the caliphate. However, this was also the time when extravagance was at its peak. Moreover, even in later years of decline, the rulers were more indulged in luxuries and comforts. • 3. Disintegration of different areas of caliphate started and several autonomous dynasties appeared.
Decline of Abbasid Caliphate
The first such autonomous state was the Emirate of Cordoba where Umayyads became sovereign rulers in 756 AD.
End of Abbasid Dynasty

During the early 13th century Mongol Empire rose in East and North Central Asia. After conquering China, the Mongols started their campaign from west to the Middle East. This was the ill-fated year 1258 AD when the Mongols arrived at Abbasids capital Baghdad. Mongol army, led by Hulaku Khan, defeated the Muslims under the last caliph in Baghdad Mu'tasim and killed not only the caliph but also thousands of people.
End of Abbasid Dynasty

Fall of Baghdad is believed to be the most devastating moment in the history of the Muslims. It was because the sack of Baghdad would mark the end of the Islamic Golden Age. The Mongols destroyed almost every building in Baghdad including masjids, palaces, and markets. The world-famous House of Wisdom and great library of Baghdad were also destroyed completely.
End of Abbasid Dynasty
Thousands of manuscripts were either burnt or thrown into the river which turned black with ink.
Facts to Know

The unfortunate year (1258 AD) is considered to be the end of Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad. However, in 1261 AD, the Abbasids reclaimed the Caliphate from Egypt. The real power in Egypt was with the Mamluks who ran affairs of the state. Together they ruled the Caliphate from Cairo until 1517 when they were conquered by the Ottomans.

The Seljuk (1037-1243 AD)

The Seljuk (taking its name from one of its chiefs, Seljuk) were one of the nomadic tribes of central Asia. Sharing a background of strong warrior tradition, Seljuk were a subdivision of the Kiniq clan of the Oghuz Turks. In the 10th century they nomadized in the steppes to the east Caspian Sea and north of the Aral Sea. It was in middle of 10th century that Seljuk and his followers embraced Islam.
The Seljuk (1037-1243 AD)
The Seljuk established a dynastic empire in the 11th century. This empire expanded from Anatolia to Punjab including most of modern-day Iran, Afghanistan, and Middle East. Seljuk died in 1007.
The Seljuk (1037-1243 AD)
By the mid-1020s, the Seljuks crossing the Kara Kum steppes reached Ghaznavid province of Khurasan.
Do You Know?
The Seljuk military and state governance systems were the most advanced of their time.

Mahmud of Ghazna took this movement as a danger. The Seljuks and Ghaznavids were involved in long power struggle over the region until Tughril and his brother Chaghri, the grandsons of Seljuk defeated the Ghaznavids. They captured Nishapur, the capital of Ghaznavid Khurasan. This led to foundation of Seljuk Empire.
The Seljuk (1037-1243 AD)

By 1055, Tughril Beg conquered Iraq where Caliph gave him the title of Sultan and tasked him to combat the Fatimids of Egypt. Tughril Beg died in 1063 in Ray and was succeeded by his nephew (Chaghri Begh's Son), Alp Arslan.
Alp Arslan

Alp Arslan, the son of Chaghri Beg, annexed Armenia and Georgia in 1064. He invaded the Byzantine Empire in 1068, and captured Anatolia. In 1071 Alp Arslan neutralized the Byzantine threat through decisive victory in the Battle of Manzikert, Turkmen generals carved their own principalities out of formerly Byzantine Anatolia.
Malik Shah

Alp Arslan was succeeded by his son Malik Shah in 1072. Under Malik Shah the empire reached its territorial peak extending its lands from Syria to Yemen and from Anatolia to China. It had the Jerusalem, Damascus, Aleppo, Mosul, Antioch, and Baghdad under its (continues on the next page)

However, rebellion and war with neighbouring kingdoms led to weakening the Empire. The Assassins of Hassan-i Sabah became very powerful who assassinated many leading figures in his administration.
Government

The Seljuk empire was a group of semi-independent kingdoms instead of a centralised state. Each kingdom was ruled by a member of Seljuk family who maintained order through amirs. State administration was headed by a vizier. The army was made up of different nationalities headed by Turk commanders.
Do You Know?
Animated art (Script) was introduced by Seljuks where letters were transformed into human and animal figures.
Decline

Seljuk Empire weakened after death of Malik Shah I in 1092 and a quarrel for apportioning the successor started among his brother and sons. As he was succeeded by many, the empire split in numerous independent and unstable principalities. The fractured states were concerned more to consolidate their own territories. Court intrigue dominated the politics of the Seljuk Sultanate.

Legacy

Seljuk brought material and cultural prosperity. Architecture and the arts flourished setting the stage for future artistic developments. They brought significant social changes in the region by developing an advanced political state. Ottoman Empire and the Turkish Republic are socially, economically, and religiously indebted to the Seljuk Empire.
Fatimids (909-1171 AD)

Abu Muhammad Abdallah ibn al-Husayn, better known by his regnal name Al-Mahdi Billah was founder of Fatimid caliphate which arose out of an underground missionary movement in the 10th century. An armed rebellion against the Abbasid caliphate started in parts of Iran, Iraq, Syria, Bahrain, Yemen, and North Africa. During this time, Al-Mahdi made his way from Syria to North Africa.
Fatimids (909-1171 AD)

On capturing Qayrawan in 909 AD, Al-Mahdi declared himself to be the first Fatimid caliph. The Fatimids in North Africa sought to expand their rule with the eventual goal of overthrowing the Abbasid caliphate in Baghdad. Al-Mahdi and his son and successor al-Qa'im, made several attempts to conquer Egypt without success. The fourth Fatimid caliph, al-Mu'izz conquered Egypt in 969 AD.
Fatimids (909-1171 AD)
With Egypt as centre, the empire at its peak expanded to parts of North Africa, Sicily, Palestine, Jordan, Lebanon, Syria, Tihamah, Hejaz, Yemen, and Multan (Pakistan).
Achievements of Fatimids

Egypt became the political, cultural, and religious centre of the empire, and developed a new and "indigenous Arabic" culture. Fatimid built Cairo as capital of their empire with seminaries Al-Azhar and Darul Hikmah. Ayyubids (1171-1260 AD)

The Ayyubid Dynasty founded by Salah al-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub (Saladin) ruled Egypt, Syria-Palestine, parts of northern Mesopotamia (the Jazira) and Yemen between 1171 and 1260. Ayyubid rise to power began with two Kurdish brothers (Ayyub and Shirkuh), who migrated to Iraq in 1130 AD. They entered the service of 'Imad al-Din Zangi, the powerful Turkish governor in northern Syria.

Shirkuh served Nur al-Din Mahmud as commander of the expeditionary force in Egypt. After death of Shirkuh in 1169, power passed to his brother Ayyub's son, Salah al-Din Yusuf (Saladin) as both commander of the Syrian troops in Egypt and vizier of the Fatimid caliph there. As vizier of Egypt, he was given the title "king" (malik), although he was generally known as the sultan.

The Crusades were religious wars, sanctioned by the Roman Catholic Church in the medieval period. These wars were fought during 1095 AD–1492 AD. Roman Catholic Church launched military expeditions from Europe to Palestine, to reclaim Holy Land from the Muslims. The fighting between the Muslims and Crusaders took place in the areas of present day Palestine, Lebanon, Syria and Egypt.

The name of Ottoman Empire comes from Osman Ghazi, who was the son of Ertugrul Bey, a Seljuk Ruler. The Ottoman Empire was founded in Sogut in 1299 AD near Bursa, Turkey. Different from other Anatolian princely states, the Ottomans expanded towards the west and constantly fought against the shrinking Byzantine Empire.

The Ottoman Caliphate

The Ottoman Dynasty had 36 sultans in total and ruled for 623 years between 1299 and 1922. After the conquest of Egypt by Sultan Selim I in 1517, the caliphate passed to the Ottoman sultans and they assumed the title, "khadim al-haramain al-sharifain" (the servant of two holy sanctuaries i.e. Makkah and Madinah).
The Ottoman Caliphate
The Ottoman Caliphate continued for 407 years until it was abolished with the formation of the Republic of Turkey. There were total 30 Ottoman caliphs.
Administrative and Political System

The Ottoman State became an independent government by 1335 AD with the total collapse of the Anatolian Saljuk and Ilhanid rules in Anatolia. Most of the Ottoman government institutions were founded during the time of Orhan Ghazi and Murad I.
Central Administration

The Ottomans had a degree of central government unmatched in Europe of that time. The Ottoman sultans delegated a good deal of their authority to their viziers and other high officials of their empire. Government positions were based purely on merit.
Provincial Administration

The Ottoman Empire was subdivided into many eyalets (provinces). They were supervised by governors who were appointed by the sultan. The beylerbeyi (chief governor) of each eyalet was appointed by the central government. Eyalets were divided into sanjaks (districts) which were governed by sanjak-beys (district governors) who were selected from the high military ranks by the central government.
Provincial Administration
Beylerbeyis had authority over all the sanjak-beyis in a region. Kaza was the sub-district of sanjak governed by a kadi (local administrator).
Social Structure
The Ottoman social structure may be divided into five categories:
Social Structure

People of the Pen (scholars, physicians) • People of the Sword (military personnel) • People of Governance (executive, judiciary, bureaucracy) • People of Negotiation (merchants and tax collectors) • People of Craft (farmers, herders, and artisans)
Do You Know?

Non-Muslim communities were organised according to the millet system, that gave minority religious/ethnic/geographical communities a limited amount of power to regulate their own affairs - under the overall supremacy of the Ottoman administration.
Social Structure

The Ottoman Empire did not consist only of Muslim Turks but was a large and multi-ethnic state with people following different religions. In the Ottoman society, Muslims coexisted peacefully with Christians, Jews and the followers of other faiths. Under the millet (religious group) system, the people of each faith were ruled and judged under their own laws.
Social Structure

Even though, non-Muslims were not appointed to high offices, this regulation was not fully implemented during much of the Ottoman rule. The high number of tax-payers supported the efficient Ottoman bureaucracy.

Expansion of the Ottoman Empire

At its height, the Ottoman Empire covered a geography of 22 million square kilometres including most of south-eastern Europe to the gates of Vienna, present-day Hungary, the Balkan region, Greece, and parts of Ukraine; portions of the Middle East where now Iraq, Syria, Palestine and Egypt are; North Africa as far west as Algeria; and large parts of the Arabian Peninsula including Yemen and the Hejaz region.
Expansion of the Ottoman Empire

The largest geographical expansions made by the Ottomans were during the reigns of Sultan Muhammad Fatih – the conqueror of Constantinople. Another was Selim I – who conquered Egypt and assumed the title of Caliph. Most important was Suleyman I – called as Suleyman the Magnificent by Europeans for remaining in power for 46 years and reaching with his armies until the gates of Vienna (Austria).
Expansion of the Ottoman Empire

This wave of Ottoman expansion is known as the Classical Age of the Ottoman Empire between the Conquest of Constantinople in 1453 AD until the second half of the sixteenth century, roughly the end of the reign of Suleiman the Magnificent in 1566 AD. During this period, the Ottoman Empire developed the institutional foundations which it would keep, in various changes, for several centuries.
Expansion of the Ottoman Empire
The Ottoman Empire reached its most extensive boundaries in 1699 AD.
The Ottoman Influence on World Politics

The Ottoman Empire, during its glorious days, was the world's superpower. It influenced the regional and global politics by its military might, administrative strength, and most importantly its commonwealth of nations, who peacefully coexisted in a large geography. The Ottoman sultans were considered the nightmare of the tyrants and the saviour of the oppressed.
The Ottoman Influence on World Politics

The Ottoman Empire left a deep political impact on three continents at multiple levels. Not only the Ottoman land forces, also the Ottoman Navy made an impact on European, African and Middle Eastern powers.
The Ottoman Influence on World Politics

Four Ottoman Sultans – Muhammad Fatih, Selim I, Suleyman the Magnificent and Murad III – were very influential, by their expansive conquests and political agreements with several European kingdoms to divide them politically.
The Ottoman Influence on World Politics

Another political impact of the Ottomans was Selim I's consolidation of the Arab States under Ottoman rule, thus effectively securing the Middle East against attacks from Europe. Selim I's son Suleyman the Magnificent focused on Europe and established himself as the most powerful man in the world.

Muslims in South Asia

Islam came to South Asia and Southeast Asia through Arab traders. Arabs had trade relations with India before arrival of Islam. Merchants would regularly sail to the west coast of India to trade goods such as spices, gold, and African goods. When Arabs converted to Islam, they introduced their new religion to India. Islam continued to spread in India through Arab traders missionaries, and conversion.
Muslims in South Asia
During Pious caliphate, attempts were made to annex Sindh but it could not be occupied.
Muslims in South Asia

The relations between the Arabs and the Indians were smooth. However, the sea borne trade of the Arabs in the Indian Ocean was threatened by Raja Dahir. To overcome the challenges by Raja Dahir and his allies, Hajjaj Bin Yusuf, the governor of Basra, Sent Muhammad Bin Qasim in 712 AD. After capturing Debal, the strong hold of Dahir, he moved to Aror where Dahir was killed.
Muslims in South Asia
With the conquest of Multan, the entire Sindh fell under Arab rule and remained so for the next three centuries.

Mansura was the historic capital of the Muslim Caliphate in Sindh from the year 711 to 1006 AD. The city was founded as a central garrison by the Umayyad Forces in Sindh. Later the city transformed into a very dynamic metropolis.
The Ghaznavids (977-1186 AD)

Relations between Arabia and the Subcontinent increased gradually. Unfortunately, as the years went by, the leadership in Arabia grew weaker. This allowed many local governors of Sindh to break free from the Arab rule and become independent. When Sultan Mehmud of Ghazna invaded South Asia, only two Muslim states were existing with headquarters in Multan and Mansura.
The Ghaznavids (977-1186 AD)

The Ghaznavids rose to power in Ghazna which is situated in present day Afghanistan. Mehmud Ghaznavi was the most important ruler of the Ghaznavi dynasty. He ruled between 998 and 1030 AD. Overall, the Ghaznavid Empire lasted for 157 years.
Mehmud Ghaznavi's Invasions of South Asia

Mehmud Ghaznavi is considered among one of the mightiest kings in the Muslim history. He was born in 927 AD. Mehmud Ghaznavi became a king when he was about 26. Mehmud's major rule was in Afghanistan, but he added many areas of South Asia to his empire. Mehmud Ghaznavi attacked and invaded South Asia about seventeen times. Each time he emerged victorious because of his successful war strategies.
Ghauris in India

His most well-known conquest was that of Somnath in 1024 AD. Somnath was a city in Gujrat, Kathiawar, and was ruled by a Hindu king Bhima I. This city was known for its famous temple where the Hindus used to worship their idols. Mehmud Ghaznavi launched a massive attack on Somnath in 1026 AD. Despite facing resistance from surrounding Rajput rulers, he conquered the city.
Impacts of Mehmud Ghaznavi's Victories

Mehmud's invasion played an important role in the spreading of Islam in India. • India's enormous wealth was taken away to Ghazni. • Mehmud's conquests paved the way for the Muslim conquest of India. • The weaknesses of local Indian rulers were exposed and that made India more unstable. • Sultan Mehmud Ghaznavi did not consolidate his empire by establishing any organized administration.
Impacts of Mehmud Ghaznavi's Victories
Soon, the empire fell in the hands of his weak successors and gradually lost control of Indian territories.

The Ghauris belonged to Afghanistan. After the decline of the Ghaznavi's, they rose to power.
Ghauris in India

Muhammad Ghauri was the younger brother of the governor of Ghazna. He was determined to establish Muslim rule in South Asia. Sultan Ghauri started his military expedition by capturing Peshawar. After several years of attempts, he defeated the ruler of Punjab, Khusro Malik, and annexed Punjab to the Muslim Empire. Historians agree that the battles of Tarain were the most difficult battles Sultan Ghauri fought.

Iltutmish

Shams-ud-din Iltutmish was the third ruler of Slave Dynasty. He was a slave and after multiple sales he was purchased by Qutbuddin Aibak. Iltutmish

He introduced a sound administrative set up. He successfully tackled the Mongols. He played very important role in consolidation of Slave Dynasty and Muslim Rule in India. He was succeeded by her daughter Razia Sultan in 1236 AD.

Razia Sultan (1236-1240 AD)

Razia Sultan succeeded her father as the heir of the throne instead of her brothers. This decision was met by opposition. She had to face many challenges from powerful nobles who were not willing to accept a woman as a ruler despite her qualities. The nobles wanted a puppet ruler who could govern according to their wishes. But Razia Sultan refused to do so. Many attempts were made to depose her from the throne.
Razia Sultan (1236-1240 AD)

Razia Sultan's rule lasted for about four years. Her rule was successful in a limited sense as she was able to restore peace throughout the kingdom by diplomacy. She appointed an Abyssinian slave named Yaqut to a high position, causing anger among the nobles. This reduced her support in court matters.
Achievements

1. She was the first women ruler of Delhi. • 2. As the first Muslim women ruler, she holds a great significance in the Indian history. • 3. She bravely attacked the enemy territories and merged them with the sultanate to strengthen the Kingdom. • 4. She brought many reforms to the administration. She was a skilled diplomat of her time. • 5. She opened libraries to promote knowledge.

Razia Sultan, the first Muslim women ruler in South Asia and is commonly known as Razia.

i. He protected his empire from Mongols attacks. • ii. He stabilized his kingdom and took strict action against government's corruption and potential rebellions.

Balban served the Delhi sultanate as Sultan for 40 years. He established peace in the empire and resisted the Mongol invaders successfully. The Khilji Dynasty (1290-1320 AD)

The Khilji dynasty ruled large parts of the Indian Subcontinent between 1290 and 1320 AD. It was founded by Jalal-ud-Din Feroz Khilji and became the second dynasty to rule the Delhi Sultanate of India.
Alauddin Khilji

He ruled as Sultan of Delhi from 1296-1316 AD. Alauddin Khilji ascended to the throne after eliminating the Sultan Jalal-ud-Din Feroz Khilji. As a ruler, he proved himself to be one of India's greatest warrior kings and one of the world's great military geniuses.
Alauddin Khilji Defence Policies Against Mongol Invasions

During the reign of Alauddin Khilji. Mongols invaded India seven times, but Alauddin succeeded in defeating them every time. Alauddin Khilji planned to defend the empire by formulating a strong and systematic frontier policy.
Alauddin Khilji Defence Policies Against Mongol Invasions

i. Old forts were restored, new forts were built and skilled troops under capable officers were posted. Their military power was also enhanced. • ii. Factories were set up to produce armaments. • iii. A permanent army was organized for the defence of the North-West Frontier and a special governor was appointed there. • iv. Separate armies were stationed in the frontier areas of Dipalpur, Samana and Multan.
Alauddin Khilji Defence Policies Against Mongol Invasions
Alauddin's frontier policy proved very successful. The Mongols ceased their aggression during the later years of Alauddin's reign.

Tughluq's Rise to Power (1320-1413 AD)

After the death of Alauddin Khilji in 1316, first Malik Kafur and then Mubarak Shah seized the throne. Both were murdered one after another leaving Khusrau Khan, the favourite slave of Mubarak Shah as the Sultan. He could not win the favour of people who invited Governor of Punjab, Ghazi Khan for help. He revolted against Mubarak Khan and sat on the throne himself.
Tughluq's Rise to Power (1320-1413 AD)
Ghazi Khan is known as Ghias-ud-Din Tughluq Shah who laid the basis of Tughluq Dynasty in 1320 AD.
Tughluq's Rise to Power (1320-1413 AD)

Tughluq Shah was one of the most trusted generals of Alauddin Khilji. He proved his skills by successfully defending against Mongols. He ruled the Sultanate skilfully and peace prevailed during his reign. Ghias-ud-Din patronized literary men like Amir Khusrau. He also built a strong fort called Tughluqabad near Delhi.
Invasions of Taimur

After the death of Ghias-ud-Din, his son Jauna Khan succeeded in 1325 AD. In history, he is known with the title of Muhammad bin Tughluq. During his 26 years of rule, the sultanate witnessed peak of prosperity. Few of his experiments were not successful. These included introduction of copper coins, shifting of capital from Delhi to Daulatabad and back to Delhi.
Invasions of Taimur

After Muhammad bin Tughluq his nephew Feroz Shah Tughluq ruled for 37 years. After his death in 1338 civil war started among his successors. Feroz Tughluq was succeeded by one of his grandsons, Tughluq Shah, who assumed the title of Ghias- ud-Din Tughluq II. Within few months he was assassinated.
Invasions of Taimur

During the next five years, three Sultans- Abu Bakr, Muhammad Shah and Alauddin Sikander Shah became rulers one after another. The last Tughluq ruler, Nasir-ud-Din Mahmud Shah remained the ruler for 18 years. It was during his rule when Taimur invaded and Tughluq Dynasty came to an end.

Invasions of Taimur

Taimur was a Turko-Mongol conqueror who brought most of the Muslim-ruled parts of Central Asia and India under his control in the 14th century. He was the founder of the Taimurid empire of Central Asia, ultimately ruling much of Europe and Asia.
Invasions of Taimur

The unsettled political conditions in South Asia encouraged Taimur to attempt to invade. He therefore sent his grandson Pir Muhammad with a large army to launch an attack on India. The attack proved successful and Multan and Uch were captured. Following this victory, Taimur gathered an army of 92000 and marched towards Delhi, where he was joined by Pir Muhammad.
Invasions of Taimur

There, they faced Nasir-Ud-Din Tughluq and his army with nearly 1000 war elephants. Although frightened by the sight of such huge creatures, the leaders kept calm and devised several war strategies that enabled them to win the battle. Overall, Taimur's invasions had deep impacts on the Subcontinent.

Causes of Downfall of the Delhi Sultanate

The Delhi Sultanate lasted for a period of 320 years from 1206 to 1526 AD. The decline started earlier and completed in 1526. There were many factors behind this downfall. Few important ones are as under:
Causes of Downfall of the Delhi Sultanate

1. No law of succession made the transition to throne a matter of conflict. Death of a Sultan normally resulted in civil war. • 2. Over the years, the empire had extended significantly. Without effective means of communication, it became difficult to keep effective control from the centre. • 3. Poor administration of revenue led to wide-scale corruption in the state affairs. This ultimately weakened the sultanate.
Causes of Downfall of the Delhi Sultanate

• 4. Nobles rebelled against weak rulers. • 5. Regional states became very powerful in 15th century. They refused to pay revenue and thus made it difficult for the center to keep control on them. • 6. Taimur's attack was a big blow to the rulers of Delhi and Babur's invasion proved to be last nail in the coffin of Sultanate.

Sufism in Subcontinent

Following advent of Islam in South Asia in early 8th century Sufism formed its way to this region during Delhi Sultanate. Hazrat Usman bin Ali Hujwiri was the first important Sufi who made India his home. Sufism is based on concept of love of Allah. Followers of Sufism search for closeness to God, knowledge, spiritual truth and ultimate reality through intuition and insight.
Sufism in Subcontinent

Sufism came into being in 8th century in reaction to increasing worldliness among the Muslims when they got power over large part of the globe. Sufism played an important role in formation of Muslim society through educating the masses. Efforts were directed towards creation of a healthy social order, free from conflicts. The Sultans of Delhi and later on Mughal Kings patronized Sufism.
Tasawuf

Tasawuf is an Arabic word meaning "to dress in wool" used by Muslim as part of their clothing and simple living. Tasawuf was called Sufism in western languages since early 19th century. The word Sufi has been derived from Suf meaning "wool".

The Sufis tried to bring peace and harmony in the multiracial and multireligious Indian society. Sufi saints of that time are revered even today by not only Muslims but by a large number of Hindus, and their tombs have become popular places of pilgrimage for both communities.

Foundation of The Mughal Empire

Long before the establishment of the Mughal Empire, Turko-Afghan dynasties, known as Delhi Sultanate, were founded. They ruled South Asia for about 300 years. In 1398 AD, the Turks, led by the fierce conqueror Taimur the Lame, attacked northern India and appointed Khizr Khan as governor of the conquered territories. Within a century, the northern India disintegrated into a collection of small kingdoms.
Foundation of The Mughal Empire
In the early 16th century, powerful Mughals invaded India. In this unit, you will learn about the establishment of the Mughal Empire and its legacy.
Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur

The founder of the Mughal Empire was Zahiruddin Muhammad Babur (1526 AD -1530 AD). Babur was a brilliant general who descended from both Taimur and Genghis Khan. Babur achieved some major successes against Ibrahim Lodhi, Afghans, Rajputs and founded the Mughal Empire.
Consolidation of the Mughal Empire

By 1529 AD, Babur successfully conquered the major parts of northern India and began consolidating the Mughal Empire. The boundaries for the Mughal Empire were defined by the natural topography of the Subcontinent. Babur also made some of the following important efforts to develop an efficient administration of the Empire:
Babur's Memoirs

1. Babur built Agra as his capital. He gathered support of the nobles by presenting them lands as gifts. • 2. He appointed his four sons as governors to administer the provinces proficiently. • 3. The Hindus and the Muslims both were made a part of the local administration.

Nasiruddin Muhammad Humayun

Babur was succeeded by his son Nasiruddin Muhammad Humayun 1530 AD–1556 AD as a Mughal ruler of India. Humayun ruled twice from 1530 AD to 1540 AD and again from 1555AD to 1556 AD. Some historians view Humayun as a weak ruler because during his time, some Indian rulers seized the opportunity and dethroned Humayun for more than a decade. Sher Shah Suri was one of those challengers to Humayun's rule.
The Afghan Interruption

Sher Shah Suri of Pashtun sub tribe rose against Humayun in 1539 AD and 1540 AD. Sher Shah Suri defeated Humayun both the times in the battle and founded the Suri Empire in the northern parts of India. Humayun not only lost the control of the Empire, but he had also lost his throne. Consequently, in 1540 AD, Humayun had to go into forced exile and Sher Shah Suri occupied the throne of Delhi.
The Rule of Sher Shah Suri (1540 AD -1545 AD)

Although Sher Shah Suri's rule did not last more than five years but his reign proved to be a milestone in the administrative history of the Subcontinent. Here is a glance at some of his accomplishments.
The Rule of Sher Shah Suri (1540 AD -1545 AD)

Sher Shah Suri had a number of ministers to assist him in his administrative work. • Sher Shah Suri employed a powerful army. • Law and order in the kingdom were improved by strictly dealing with decoits and theifs. • The protection of traders on roads enhanced trade and commerce in the empire. • He set up a simple tax collection system.
The Rule of Sher Shah Suri (1540 AD -1545 AD)
He abolished the old and mixed metal currency and introduced gold and silver coins. • The land tax on peasants was levied according to their income. Later, the British also adopted this system.
Restoration of the Mughal Empire and Akbar

Internal trade taxes were abolished. • Numerous civil works were carried out including planting of trees, wells and building of Sarai (inns) for travelers. • Roads were laid; it was under his rule that the Grand Trunk Road from Delhi to Kabul was rebuilt.
Do You Know?
Qila Rohtas was built by Sher Shah Suri in 16th century. It is located on GT Road near city of Jhelum in Punjab. It is an exceptional example of Muslim military architecture in Subcontinent.
Restoration of the Mughal Empire and Akbar

Sher Shah Suri lost his life in an accident during the siege of Kalinjar fort in Uttar Perdesh on May 13, 1545 AD. Sher Shah Suri's successors, however, proved to be weak and incapable rulers. The Mughals were able to establish their rules in India after a few days.
Humayun's Victory and Death

Humayun took advantage of the disputes among Sher Shah Suri's successors and returned to India. He recaptured Lahore, Delhi and Agra and regained the throne in 1555 AD with the help of the emperor of Persia, Shah Tahmasp- I. Humayun made Delhi his capital and immediately began to reorganize his empire. Six months after regaining power, he fell down the stairs of his library in Delhi and died.
Humayun's Victory and Death
He was succeeded by his son Akbar.
Jalalud Din Muhammad Akbar (1556 AD-1605 AD)

During the years of Humayun's exile in Persia, Akbar was raised among tough warriors in Afghanistan. Although he could not learn to read and write formally but he was eager to acquire new ideas from people who visited his court.
Note for Teachers

Expansion and Consolidation of Mughal Empire by Akbar's Conquests
Being a great warrior, Akbar established a vast kingdom by conquering following kingdoms:
Expansion and Consolidation of Mughal Empire by Akbar's Conquests

He captured Gwalior, Ajmer, Jaunpur and Malwa. He also succeeded in capturing the famous forts of Ranthambhore and Chittor. • Military campaigns in Gujarat were followed by campaigns in the east in Bihar, Bengal, and Orissa. Akbar's armies also conquered Kandahar, Kashmir, Sindh and Balochistan. • From 1595 AD to 1601 AD, Akbar's forces annexed some of the Deccan sultanates namely Berar and Ahmednagar.
Akbar's Policy toward Rajputs

Rajputs were the most powerful rivals of the Mughals in North India. Akbar recognized the fact that there could be no permanent Mughal rule in India without the support of the Rajputs. Knowing this, Akbar developed friendly relationship with Rajput states instead of conquering them.
Akbar's Policy toward Rajputs
He also took certain measures such as alliances and assigning higher posts to Rajput chiefs which strengthened Akbar's position as their ruler.
Do You Know?
Akbar married a Hindu princess, Hira Kunwari. She was given the title of Mariam-uz-Zamani on birth of Jehangir.
Establishment of Good Governance
In addition to being a military genius, Akbar also proved to be a successful leader and administrator. He divided the empire into fifteen provinces and appointed governors for an effective control.
Financial Reforms

An efficient system of taxation was introduced in which the rich were taxed more than the poor. • Agricultural area was increased for better crop output. • Indian peasants were required to pay about one-third of their annual harvest to the state, but the system was applied justly. When bad weather struck in the 1590s, taxes were reduced or suspended altogether. • Trade and manufacturing industry flourished.
Financial Reforms
Indian goods, especially textiles, tropical food products, tropical spices, and precious stones were exported in exchange for gold and silver.
Mansabdari System

In 1570 AD, Mansabdari System was introduced as a new administrative and revenue system. Mansabdars were directly accountable to the emperor. They were responsible to collect the land revenue and all other taxes. Military responsibilities of Mansabdars were to maintain a specified number of cavalrymen, to get them registered and their horses trademarked.
Mansabdari System
This was meant to reinforce the emperor's military power during wars.
Religious Reforms

Akbar followed liberal views towards religion. He used to hold discussions with the leaders of different religions. Akbar adopted a policy of religious tolerance based on honesty, justice, and peace. He believed that all religions taught similar beliefs and ideals.
Religious Reforms

Abul Fazl, Akbar's friend and counsellor, helped Akbar in framing the idea of one common religion so that he could govern a diverse Indian society effectively and peacefully. Indeed, Akbar incorporated the principles of different religions to found a new faith which he named Din-i-Illahi. Muslims clergy completely disapproved of Akbar's new religion.
Religious Reforms
Din-i-Illahi' did not attract many converts and it perished with the death of Akbar.
Note for Teachers

Inform the students that the Deccan Sultanates were five late- medieval Indian kingdoms on the Deccan Plateau that were ruled by Muslim dynasties: namely Ahmadnagar, Berar, Bidar, Bijapur, and Golkonda.
Jahangir

The long and glorious rule of Akbar came to an end in Agra in 1605 AD. Akbar on his deathbed confirmed his eldest son Salim as his successor. The new emperor chose the Persian name Jahangir, meaning 'World Seizure' as his title.
Nur-ud-din Jahangir (1605 - 1628 AD)

Nur-ud-din Muhammad Salim often called Prince Salim was the fourth Mughal Ruler. He was Akbar's son by a Rajput wife. He ascended throne on his father's death in 1605. His ascension was challenged by his eldest son Khusrau who revolted against him. The revolt was put down however it led to execution of fifth Sikh Guru Arjun Dev. This resulted an increase in tension between Mughals and Sikhs.
Influence of Nur Jahan

The emperor Jahangir was married to Mehr-un- Nisa who assumed the title of Nur Jahan. She was a daughter of one of his ministers. Owing to her beauty and intelligence, she gained influence on Jahangir and had the opportunity to play a direct role in the affairs of the empire. She was also actively involved in the political and military affairs.
Influence of Nur Jahan
Nur Jahan became the real power behind the Mughal throne during Jahangir's reign.
Contributions of Nur-ud-din Muhammad Jahangir

The emperor Jahangir was involved in conquests aimed at expanding the territories under Mughal's rule. He successfully ended the war with the Rajput princedom of Mewar in 1614 AD. In 1622 AD, he sent his son Prince Khurram (later known as Shah Jahan), to fight against the combined forces.
Do You Know?
On become successor, Nur-ud-din Muhammad Salim gave himself Persian name Jahangir (World Seizer). He permitted the British to trade in India which ultimately led to end of Mughal Rule in India.
Art and Architecture During Jahangir's Reign
Apart from strengthening the military power, Jahangir and Nur Jahan also gave importance to art, architecture, and other important works.
Note for Teachers

Abul Fazl was a court historian and a noble during Akbar's reign. He wrote Akbar-Nama which was illustrated by the court artists. Akbar-Nama contains enormous details of life in the court and in his empire.
Shah Jahan
Following are some of the achievements of Jahangir:
Shah Jahan

Jahangir was a great patron of art and literature. He spent lavishly in building splendid buildings, gardens, and mausoleums. • The Mughal painting flourished during his reign. • The emperor was also known for his architectural work in variety of stones and marbles. • Other major works of his time include the construction of Masajid, Sarais (Inns), and wells on the roadsides.
Shah Jahan
Tuzuk-i-Jahangiri or Jahanghir Nama is the autobiography of Mughal Emperor Jahanghir. It includes the details like his ideas on art, politics, and information about his family.
Do You Know?

Chain of Justice: Jahangir is famous for installing the golden "Chain of Justice" outside the castle of Agra. The chain was meant to be a link between the citizens and the emperor. Jahangir announced that any aggrieved person ringing the bells would be granted a meeting with the emperor.
Shahabuddin Shah Jahan

Shah Jahan ascended the throne of Mughal Empire in 1628 AD and continued the policies of the Great Mughal rulers. He extended the Mughal rule into the South of India by conquering the Deccan states. Shah Jahan reinforced the empire by building a massive army. It is said that his army consisted of a huge number of soldiers. He also made advancement of cannons at large scale.
Patron of Arts

Shah Jahan was fond of arts and architecture. Some of the most beautiful buildings of the Mughal period were built during his time such as the Red Fort, Taj Mahal and the tomb of his wife; Mumtaz Mahel. Shah Jahan created a wonderful blend of Persian and Indian culture in the Mughal arts and architectural works.
Do You Know?

Shah Jahan built a new capital, Shahjahanabad, with its magnificent Red Fort. In the Hall of Public Audience, Shah Jahan sat on the Peacock Throne, which consisted entirely of jewels and precious metals and stones.
Do You Know?

Four legs of gold supported the seat; 12 pillars of emeralds held up the emerald canopy, each pillar bore two peacocks encrusted with gems and between each pair of peacocks rose a tree covered with diamonds, emeralds, rubies, and pearls.
Shah Jahan's Architectural Legacy
1. Taj Mahal, Agra • 2. Masjid Wazir Khan, Lahore • 3. Shalimar Bagh, Lahore • 4. Palaces in Lahore Fort • 5. Red Fort Delhi • 6. Jama Masjid, Delhi
Shah Jahan's Architectural Legacy

In September 1657 AD Shah Jahan fell ill, triggering a struggle for succession between his four sons; Dara Shikoh, Murad Bakhsh, Shah Shuja, and Aurangzeb Alamgir. The victor, Aurangzeb Alamgir, declared himself emperor in 1658 AD and strictly confined Shah Jahan in Agra Fort until his death.
Aurangzeb Alamgir: The Last of the Great Mughals

Aurangzeb Alamgir is considered the last great Mughal ruler. His rule lasted for almost fifty years 1658 AD - 1707 AD. When he became Emperor, he inherited a magnificent empire, splendid cities, forts and palaces. Aurangzeb was an eminent scholar. He knew Arabic, Persian, Turkish and Sanskrit. Like other Mughal Princes, he was trained in calligraphy and art.
Aurangzeb Alamgir: The Last of the Great Mughals
Under his rule, the Mughal empire expanded to the parts of Afghanistan and Burma.
Do You Know?

Aurangzeb 's original name was Muhi-al-Din Muhammad. His kingly title was Alamgir meaning "Jewel in the Throne". He was born in 1618 AD, at Dhod, Malwa in India. He was crowned as an Emperor in 1658 AD and he died in 1707 AD.
Aurangzeb Alamgir: The Last of the Great Mughals

Historians divide Aurangzeb's reign into two parts. In the first part of his reign i.e. until 1680 AD, he was devoted to safeguarding the empire from rebellions and disintegration. After 1680 AD, Aurangzeb seemed to have changed his policies and attitude and became very strict. As you read this unit you will discover some of the ways in which Aurangzeb changed the traditions of Mughal rulers before him.
Consolidation of Mughal Empire

Aurangzeb was a fearless warrior and respected by all for his bravery. He fought many battles against other kingdoms in order to annex them to the Mughal Empire. These are some of the important battles:
Consolidation of Mughal Empire

From 1664 AD to 1666 AD, Aurangzeb dispelled Assamese rebellion to re-establish Mughal prestige in the east of India. • Afghan tribes also caused a heavy defeat on Mughal army in the north east of India between 1667 AD and 1674 AD. Later in 1674 AD, Aurangzeb himself led the campaign and defeated the Afghans in a fierce battle.
Unpopular Policies of Aurangzeb

In 1686-87 AD, Aurangzeb occupied the kingdoms of Deccan, Bijapur and Golconda. • Another big challenge for Aurangzeb was the growing power of Marathas in the South of India. They were fierce fighters. Aurangzeb succeeded in crushing these revolts and their leader surrendered to Emperor's forces.
Unpopular Policies of Aurangzeb
According to some historians, some of the Aurangzeb's policies caused serious discontent among the Muslims and the non-Muslims alike. These policies were:
Unpopular Policies of Aurangzeb

Financial difficulties of the empire increased due to the policy of long-drawn wars of Aurangzeb. He imposed heavy taxes including war tax on the common people which were beyond their means. The wealth of the empire was reduced because farming, trade and industry were not flourishing all across India.
Unpopular Policies of Aurangzeb

• Aurangzeb wanted to unite the Subcontinent under his own politico-religious will which caused problems for his rule. For instance, Aurangzeb brought back Jizya tax on Hindus and other non-Muslims which was abolished by Akbar. Hindus were not happy at having to pay Jizya.
Note for Teachers

Inform the students that the Marathas were Hindu warriors from the Deccan located in the south of India. They caused Aurangzeb and his successors many difficulties as they invaded Mughal lands. They signed a peace treaty with Aurangzeb in 1665 AD, but it dissolved soon after. Later in 1681 AD, the Marathas became so troublesome that Aurangzeb moved to Deccan to fight against them.
Note for Teachers
However Aurangzeb could never eliminate them completely
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers

Despite all the challenges, Aurangzeb maintained the empire for nearly half a century, yet it was heading towards its downfall rapidly. After the death of Aurangzeb, the empire was facing a number of menacing administrative and economic problems. As we know from history, Mughals followed the Timurid custom of joint heirship or a division of the inheritance amongst all the sons.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers
This was meant to administer the empire effectively. Historians believe that the failure of Aurangzeb's sons to cope with the challenges prompted the decline of Mughal empire in the mid-18th century.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers

During the 16th and 17th centuries, the Mughal Empire reached the climax of its political power and culture. The Mughal rulers were not only fond of arts, architecture, and poetry, but also recognized for their high level of religious tolerance.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers
Most of the Mughal rulers ensured the balance of different socio- economic and political interests of Indian groups and communities with no interference in their religious beliefs.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers

The Mughal rulers adopted distinct ways to create religious harmony among the Muslims and non- Muslims for peaceful coexistence and smooth progress of the empire. The table on the next page represents the religious policy of the Great Mughal rulers in the Indian subcontinent.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers

Mughal Rulers | Religious Policy; Babur & Humayun | Babur practiced an open-minded and tolerant Islam. According to historians, he never persecuted the followers of other religions. Babur always valued the scholarly religious discussion. Babur's son, Humayun, also followed the religious policy of his father.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers

To a great extent, he was just as tolerant as Babur was.; Akbar & Jahanghir | Akbar was religiously most tolerant among all the Mughal rulers. He did not force Islamic laws on non-Muslim subjects and allowed them to apply the laws of their own religion to their area. As a manifestation of his religious tolerance, he also abolished the Jizya tax upon non -Muslims.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers

When Akbar's son Jahangir came to the throne, he preferred comparatively stronger religious policies. However, he remained tolerant toward all the other religions in the Empire.; Shah Jahan & Aurangzeb | Shah Jahan was unprejudiced towards all Muslim sects and non-Muslims. Many historians believe that Aurangzeb was tolerant towards all the other religions.
Religious Policy of the Mughal Rulers
He even gave charities and funds to non-Muslims for the building of their worship places. However, some historians label Aurangzeb as intolerant towards non-Muslims.

Contributions of Mughals in Art and Architecture

Apart from religious and social enlightenment of the Indian Society, the Mughal dynasty widely displayed remarkable art forms and mixed Islamic and Indian architectural styles. Mughal architecture started to flourish from the reign of Akbar until the early 18th century. Some examples of the Mughal art and architecture can be found in Pakistan, Afghanistan, India, Nepal and Bangladesh.
Forts, Palaces and Mausoleums

During the Mughal rule, the architecture of forts and tombs presented an outstanding resemblance to the Islamic architecture. The Mughals merged the Persian and Indian styles in their architecture. Forts had distinct domes, lustrous towers at corners and magnificent halls. The forts had arrangements for soldier barracks, private and public halls for meetings, horse and elephant stables and gardens at the entrance.
Forts, Palaces and Mausoleums

Delicate ornamentation with arches, decorative sections with fine geometrical designs and inscriptions were major highlights. Mughal palaces reflected beautiful craftsmanship and inspirations of Indo-Persian traditions.

Mughal Art and Literature
The mausoleum such as Taj Mahal presents a blend of Persian, Turkish and Indian style of architecture. The Mughal architecture expresses a beautiful sense of harmony and a feeling of immense peace.
Paintings

The Mughal Era has vastly contributed an admirable architectural, literary and cultural history to India. The Mughals' keen interest in paintings presented a blend of Indo-Persian mixture. The paintings of the Mughal Era show themes from stories of Persian literature and Indian folklore.
Paintings

Education In Mughal Era

During the Mughal period, the major centres of learning were located at Lahore, Delhi, Ajmer, Sialkot, Multan, Ahmadabad, Allahabad, Lucknow, Murshidabad and Deccan. Many scholars were attracted to these institutions from Persia and the Central Asia. Education was free of cost. Islamic schools were attached to the Masajid and Khanqahs of the Sufis. Persian was the official language in the Maktabs.
Education In Mughal Era
The system of education was called Nizamiyah which became popular during the later days of the Mughals. Hindu Patshalas were also set up for imparting religious instructions.
Disintegration of the Mughal Empire

Despite ruling the empire successfully for about three centuries by great Mughals, the Mughal Empire started to disintegrate after the death of Aurangzeb Alamgir in 1707. Throughout the era of later Mughals, the empire was governed in succession by incapable, weak and dissolute monarchs. They accelerated the process of disintegration of the empire and, finally led to its collapse.
Disintegration of the Mughal Empire
Fundamentally, historians agree on the following long-standing problems which the later Mughals could not deal with:
Disintegration of the Mughal Empire

The Zamindars and Nobility got corrupted and gained more power. The Mughal emperors tried to break their power but they could not succeed. • The wars of succession were prompted by succession crisis as there was no designated crown prince according to Mughal laws. Since the government system of the empire was based on dynasty, the wars among the sons or claimants of throne were likely to ensue.
Disintegration of the Mughal Empire

Only the 'strength of the sword' and support of the courtiers determined the successor. • The repeated wars of succession, internal conflicts and rebellions allowed other claimants of power to gain control over the parts of declining empire. Later Mughals could not even regain their control over the lost territories.
Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712 AD)

Bahadur Shah-I followed a policy of compromise and tried to reconcile with Rajputs, Marathas, Jats and the Sikhs who became very powerful. However, Bahadur Shah's policy of compromise ended in a failure which precipitated the decline of the Mughal Empire. After ruling for less than five years, Bahadur Shah-I was succeeded by his son Jahandar Shah in 1712, whose reign was even less fortunate than his father's.
Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712 AD)
Nevertheless, Mughal rule continued to exist.
Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712 AD)

As a matter of fact, the unsettled political and military conditions of the Mughal Empire also attracted some foreign invaders such as Nadir Shah who was the ruler of Persia. Unfortunately, the successors of Bahadur Shah-I became mere pawns in the tussle of power of 18th-century India and ultimately failed to stop the invasions and internal rebellions.
Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712 AD)

Rule of Jahandar Shah could not continue long and in the year 1713 AD he was defeated by his nephew Farrukh Siyar who became the next ruler with the help of Syed Brothers. He ruled for the next six years when in 1719 Muhammad Shah came to throne.
Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712 AD)

Period of Muhammad Shah (from 1719 to 1748) was the period of the rise of many independent states like Bengal and Oudh. Muhammad Shah was succeeded by following rulers who were mostly inefficient as compared to the earlier Mughals:
Bahadur Shah-I (1707-1712 AD)
Ahmad Shah (1748-1754) • Alamgir II (1754-1759) • Shah Alam II (1759-1806) • Akbar II (1806-1837) • Bahadur Shah Zafar (1837-1857)

British East India Company

This was the time when fighting for throne was the most prominent feature. Wars for succession took the lives of thousands of skilled commanders and soldiers which further weakened the position of the emperor. This encouraged uprisings in many provinces. At the same time, Great Britain was enjoying the status of a superpower.
British East India Company

For their own benefits, the British East India Company which was granted trading rights in India by the Queen Elizbeth I, East India Company started interfering in the local political issues. With the passage of time, East India Company got so much influence that it established its own military bases and administrative departments.

Reasons of the Collapse of the Mughal Empire
There were many causes that led to collapse of the Mughal Empire. Most prominent ones are mentioned below:
Reasons of the Collapse of the Mughal Empire

Since there was no fixed rule of succession, the Mughal dynasty very often witnessed war between the princes after the death of a king. • Later Mughals were mostly indulged in leisure which made them pay less attention towards state affairs. • Empire was very big and modes of communication were not that strong. It was extremely difficult for a central government to keep effective administration.
Reasons of the Collapse of the Mughal Empire

• Military weakness was another important cause of decline of the Mughals. After Aurangzeb, later Mughals did not pay much attention to the strengthening of the army and became dependent upon powerful nobles and other forces. No empire can stay united in the absence of a powerful army.
Reasons of the Collapse of the Mughal Empire

During this period of decline, many independent kingdoms emerged. Provinces like Bengal and Oudh were under such independent rulers who paid no respect to the central authority of the emperor. Marathas, Sikhs and Rohillas got power in different parts. These independent kingdoms made it easy for the British to defeat them one by one until they got complete control of India in 1857.

What I have learned
